course.title: Reading and Research
course.description: How to read for argument, remember what you read, judge sources and claims, search well, make usable notes, combine sources and cite them.
course.audience: A capable adult who reads a lot but has not been taught a method for reading, searching and citing. They know basic probability and can read a chart.

paragraphs: Most of us read a great deal and were never taught how. We learned to decode words, and after that we picked up habits: start at the top, highlight what looks important, trust a page that looks careful. Those habits feel like reading well, but each of them can be tested, and when it is, highlighting turns out to mark a page without teaching you what is on it, while a careful look turns out to be something any website can supply for itself.

Reading well starts from a different habit. Every text is someone's claim, made for a reason, resting on something and written by a person or organisation with a stake in it. Reading well means asking what is claimed and on what grounds, and research is the same question asked of many texts at once, together with the work of finding the texts that would answer it best and keeping hold of what they said.

What that gives you is the ability to say why you believe something you have read, and to show someone else. A headline that halves a risk, a website with a reassuring About page and a set of studies that seem to disagree all become things you can check for yourself, and what you write from them is something a reader can follow back to every source it used.
outcomes: You'll be able to choose how to read a text for a given purpose.
You'll be able to lay out an argument and find its assumption.
You'll be able to judge a source by reading laterally and a claim by its numbers and design.
You'll be able to build a search that finds what exists and follow its citations.
You'll be able to make notes you can reuse and combine them into a synthesis.
You'll be able to cite so that a reader can follow you.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on English: Reading, Writing and Rhetoric, Logic and Reasoning, Probability and Statistics.

concepts.title: Reading purpose
concepts.summary: The reason you are reading, which sets how deeply and in what order you read.

concepts.title: Survey
concepts.summary: A first pass over headings, abstract, first and last paragraphs and figures to learn the shape before reading closely.

concepts.title: SQ3R
concepts.summary: A study method: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.

concepts.title: Claim
concepts.summary: The statement an author wants you to accept.

concepts.title: Reason
concepts.summary: A statement offered to support a claim.

concepts.title: Warrant
concepts.summary: The assumption that links the evidence to the claim.

concepts.title: Retrieval practice
concepts.summary: Recalling information from memory, which strengthens it more than rereading.

concepts.title: Spacing
concepts.summary: Spreading reviews over time rather than massing them.

concepts.title: Illusion of fluency
concepts.summary: The feeling of knowing that comes from a familiar page, which does not show you can recall it.

concepts.title: Primary source
concepts.summary: Direct evidence made by participants or from original observation or data.

concepts.title: Secondary source
concepts.summary: An analysis of primary sources.

concepts.title: Tertiary source
concepts.summary: A summary of secondary sources, such as an encyclopaedia or textbook.

concepts.title: Lateral reading
concepts.summary: Leaving a page to see what others say about its source before reading the page closely.

concepts.title: SIFT
concepts.summary: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims, quotes and media to the original context.

concepts.title: Checklist
concepts.summary: A list of features such as date and author that is easy to apply and easy to fake.

concepts.title: Relative and absolute change
concepts.summary: Relative change compares the new rate to the old; absolute change is the difference.

concepts.title: Study design
concepts.summary: Whether the study assigned the exposure (an experiment) or only observed it.

concepts.title: Number needed to treat
concepts.summary: The number of people who must receive an intervention for one to benefit: 1 divided by the absolute reduction.

concepts.title: Boolean operators
concepts.summary: AND narrows a search, OR widens it and NOT excludes.

concepts.title: Truncation
concepts.summary: A wildcard that matches word endings, as in educat* for education and educator.

concepts.title: Citation chaining
concepts.summary: Following a source's references backward and the papers that cite it forward.

concepts.title: Quotation
concepts.summary: Exact words, in quotation marks, with the page.

concepts.title: Paraphrase
concepts.summary: The idea in your own words and structure, with the source still cited.

concepts.title: Patchwriting
concepts.summary: Altering a few words of the original while keeping its structure, which is not a paraphrase.

concepts.title: Synthesis
concepts.summary: A new statement built from several sources and organised by ideas, not by source.

concepts.title: Source matrix
concepts.summary: A table with sources in rows and questions in columns.

concepts.title: Vote counting
concepts.summary: Judging a question by how many sources agree, ignoring the size and quality of each study.

concepts.title: Citation
concepts.summary: A pointer in the text to a source listed in full at the end.

concepts.title: DOI
concepts.summary: A persistent identifier that resolves to a published work.

concepts.title: Common knowledge
concepts.summary: A fact widely known and easily found in many sources, which needs no citation.

lessons.title: Reading with a purpose

lead.text: Suppose you are handed the same twenty-page article on three different days. On the first you need the year a factory opened, on the second you have to decide whether the author's case holds, and on the third you want to learn the method the author describes well enough to use it. Would you read it the same way each time? You wouldn't, and you shouldn't, because each of those reasons for reading calls for a different amount of attention in a different order.

We call the reason you are reading your **purpose**, and it is the first thing to settle, since it tells you what you will have in your hands when you finish. A fact is small and can be found with a light pass. An argument has to be followed from claim to conclusion, so it needs a close read of the whole. A method has to be rehearsed until you can do it without the page, which is why it gets the most effort of the three.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the first box is the only one that stops after a single section, so most of the time we save comes from picking the right pass for the purpose rather than from reading faster.

diagram.alt: Three purposes for reading and the pass each one needs. Find a fact calls for a survey and one section; judge an argument calls for a close read of the whole text; learn a method calls for SQ3R with recitation.

reveal.text: Headings and a contents list are written to show where things are, so a fact is usually reached in two moves: find the section, then read that section closely. The next screen names the first of those moves.

lead.text: How do you find out where a fact lives, or whether a text is worth your hour at all, without already having read it? You look at the parts of the text that were written to summarise it. A paper's title and abstract say what it claims, its headings show how it is organised, the first and last paragraphs of each section carry its main moves, and the conclusion says where it ended up. Reading just these is called a **survey**, and it usually takes a few minutes.

A survey ends in a decision, which is the point of it. You may find the text answers your question and read the one section that does, or find it argues something you need to follow closely and settle in for the whole thing, or find it has nothing for you and move on having lost five minutes rather than an afternoon.

reveal.text: You will meet this word again as the first of five steps in a method called SQ3R, which the next screen sets out.

lead.text: For a text you want to learn from, a survey is only the first step of a longer routine. **SQ3R** names it: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review. Francis P. Robinson set it out in his book *Effective Study*, published in 1946.

Why do the questions come before the reading? Because a reader with a question is reading for something, and a reader without one tends to let the words go by. After the survey you turn each heading into a question, so that a heading such as "Causes of the strike" becomes "What caused the strike?". You then read each section to answer its question, close the book and say the answer aloud or in writing, which is the **recite** step, and finally review all your answers together and again some days later.

afterFigure.text: Step through the figure to see each stage. The recite step is the one most readers skip and the one that does the most for memory.

reveal.text: Notice that two of the five steps happen before you read a single paragraph closely, and two come after.

steps.headline: Estimate how long a 12,000-word article takes at 240 words per minute.

workedSteps.text: The speed is given as words per minute, so the time in minutes is the length divided by the speed.
Put the numbers in: the length is 12,000 words and the speed is 240 words per minute.
That division gives the time, in minutes.

lead.text: The speed of 240 words per minute is an assumption we are using for the exercises, not a measured fact about you, since published averages vary with the text and the reader. What matters is the habit of estimating before you start, because a time you have said aloud tells you whether to begin now or put the reading in tomorrow's diary.

Do not expect to cut the time by training yourself to read faster. Pushing speed up tends to lower how much you take in, so the saving comes from the survey, which removes whole sections from the job. In the same way, running a highlighter across a page *marks* where you were, but it does not show that you could recall what is on it.

steps.headline: Work out how long a 300-page book takes at 25 pages a day.

workedSteps.text: The pace is pages per day, so the days needed are the pages divided by the pace.
Put in the numbers.
That division gives the time, in days.

reveal.text: Estimating after the survey, and not before, is what makes the figure honest: you are now timing the job you have chosen.

lessons.orientation: Choose a pass for a reading purpose, follow SQ3R and estimate reading time.
lessons.nextAction: Find the claim, the reasons and the unstated assumption in a short argument.

blocks.text: A 14,400-word article takes an hour at a steady 240 words a minute, and its title, abstract, headings and conclusion take a few minutes. Most of us spend the hour without spending the few minutes first: we start at the top and read on until the time runs out, so we learn what the article is for and how it is laid out only once we are most of the way through it.

Practised readers turn that round. They decide first what they are reading for, whether that is one fact, an argument they have to judge or a method they want to use, and they let that decide how much of the text they read and in what order.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose a pass for a stated purpose, put the steps of SQ3R in order and estimate how long a text will take.
intro.whyItMatters: Time spent on reading is easy to waste, and a short survey is the cheapest way to spend less of it.

recap.keyIdea: Decide why you are reading before you start, survey the text, and estimate the time so that the pass you choose fits the purpose.

blocks.text: Your purpose sets the pass, a survey reads the frame of a text in a few minutes, and for learning SQ3R adds questions before the reading and recitation after it. Time is length divided by speed, so once the survey has told you which part to read you can estimate the job honestly.

recap.nextHook: Next we take a text that argues for something and find its claim, its reasons and the assumption that holds them together.

lessons.title: Reading for argument

reveal.text: The test is to ask what each sentence is for. The claim is the one that no other sentence is working to support.

lead.text: What is the author asking us to accept? It is tempting to say the topic, which is street trees, or to take the first sentence as it comes, but a topic is not a statement and the first sentence is only sometimes the one that matters. The test is to ask which statement the others are there to support.

We call that statement the **claim**, and a statement offered in support of it a **reason**. Words such as *because*, *since* and *for* point back to a reason, and words such as *so*, *therefore* and *thus* point forward to what follows from it. These are **indicator words**, and they are the quickest way into a passage, though many arguments leave them out and you then have to ask the question yourself.

lead.text: Telling a claim from a reason is a start, but arguments have more parts than two. The philosopher Stephen Toulmin proposed, in *The Uses of Argument* (1958), a layout with six. The **grounds** are the evidence or reasons offered directly for the claim. The **warrant** is the assumption that licenses moving from those grounds to that claim. The **backing** is whatever supports the warrant, a **qualifier** limits how far the claim reaches, and a **rebuttal** names a condition under which it would fail.

Why bother with all six words? Because each of them is a place where you can press on an argument. You can ask for better grounds, ask whether the warrant holds, ask how general the claim is meant to be, or ask what the author would say to the rebuttal. A reader with only the word "claim" can say little more than "I disagree".

reveal.text: Grounds and claim are visible in the text. The warrant between them usually is not, which is the next screen's subject.

lead.text: The grounds in our example say that shaded streets stay cooler. The claim says that cities should plant trees. Is anything missing between them? Yes, because nothing yet says why a cooler street matters. The argument needs one more step, that cooler streets mean fewer heat-related illnesses, and the author never states it. That unstated step is the **warrant**.

Why is it left out? Because it is so plausible that it passes unnoticed, and that is exactly what makes it worth finding. To locate a warrant, ask what would have to be true for the grounds to be true and the claim still to fail. If the streets were cooler but nobody's health changed, the grounds would stand and the claim would have no support, so the claim depends on the warrant. Once you have said it, you can ask whether it is true and what would back it, which is a question about evidence, and not about how the passage sounds.

reveal.text: The assumption was never stated, yet the argument stops working without it. Warrants are usually found by asking what the author needs you to accept.

steps.headline: Lay out the argument: "Libraries should open on Sundays. Most people work on weekdays, so Sunday is the day they could use one."

workedSteps.text: Find the claim by asking what the other sentences are for. The second sentence is a reason for the first, so the claim is that libraries should open on Sundays.
The word "so" marks the end of the reason, and the grounds are the first half of that sentence: most people work on weekdays.
For those grounds to support the claim, people who work on weekdays have to be free to visit on a Sunday, and willing to. That unstated step is the warrant.
As written, the claim covers every library in every place.

lead.text: Two habits make readers miss the structure of an argument. The first is hearing a strong tone as strong support: a writer who says "obviously" or "no sensible person doubts" is telling us how sure they are, which is a fact about the writer, not about the grounds. The second is letting a plausible assumption go by. The more natural the warrant sounds, the less likely you are to say it aloud, and so the less likely you are to ask whether it is true.

Both are cured by the same routine. Write the claim in one sentence, list the grounds, then write the warrant in a sentence of your own and decide whether it is true, partly true or doubtful. Then ask when the claim would fail, and write that condition down as well.

reveal.text: The grounds and the backing support the argument, and the warrant joins the grounds to the claim. Only the rebuttal says when the claim would fail.
Naming that step shows where an objector would press, for example by asking for evidence that breakfast improves learning.

lessons.orientation: Find the claim, grounds and unstated warrant of a short argument.
lessons.nextAction: Use recall and spaced reviews so that what you read stays with you.

blocks.text: Here is an argument in two sentences: "Cities should plant more street trees. Shaded streets stay cooler in summer, so trees reduce heat-related illness." Most readers nod at it, since every part sounds reasonable, but ask which of those statements the author actually wants you to accept, and what else has to be true for the rest to support it, and the nod gets harder to give.

Those two questions are the heart of reading for argument. When you can say which sentence is the claim, what is offered in support of it and which step the author has left unsaid, you can agree for a reason or disagree at a definite point.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the claim and the grounds in a passage, say its unstated warrant and name where it could fail.
intro.whyItMatters: An argument you can lay out is one you can question, and that is how you avoid being carried along by tone.

recap.keyIdea: Find the claim, then the grounds, then ask what must be true for the grounds to support it: that unstated assumption is the warrant.

blocks.text: The claim is the statement the other sentences work to support, and the grounds are the reasons given for it. Between them sits a warrant, which the author usually leaves unsaid, and a qualifier and a rebuttal show how far the claim reaches and when it would fail.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at how to keep what you read, since an argument you have followed is lost quickly unless you do something with it.

lessons.title: Remembering what you read

reveal.text: The three activities that kept the page in front of you all felt easier, and that ease is the thing the next screen warns about.

lead.text: You have finished a chapter, and you have twenty minutes left. What should you do with them? Most of us reread, because it feels like work and because the page is right there, but there is a better option that feels worse. Close the book and write three sentences about what you have just read, from memory, and then open it again to check them.

Why does the harder option win? Producing an answer from memory strengthens the route to it, and failing to produce one shows you, for free, which part you do not yet have. In 2006 Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke gave students short prose passages to study and then either had them read a passage again or take a free-recall test on it. Rereaders did better on a test five minutes later, but when the final test came two days and a week after, the students who had been tested remembered more. We call this **retrieval practice**: recalling something strengthens it more than looking at it again.

afterFigure.text: Rereading ends in a feeling and recalling ends in information, and only the second tells you something you can act on.

lead.text: Why do rereading and highlighting feel so good if they work so poorly? Because a page you have read before is easy to read. The words arrive smoothly, you recognise the argument, and you conclude that you know it, but recognising something on the page is a much lower bar than recalling it when the page is gone. The feeling of knowing that a familiar page gives you, which does not show you could recall it, is called the **fluency illusion**.

The remedy is to let the test come before the feeling. After reading, try to recall without the page, and treat what you cannot recall as the useful result. Highlighting still has a job, since it marks where to return, but it is the marking that helps you navigate and not the memory it seems to leave.

reveal.text: Recognising a page and recalling its content are different tasks, which is why a test is a better judge of what you know.

lead.text: Retrieval works best when it is repeated, and when the repetitions are spread out. Spreading reviews over time rather than massing them together is called **spacing**. A gap lets you forget a little, and a retrieval that takes some effort does more than one that needs none, so reviewing a topic tomorrow, in three days, in a week and in a fortnight beats four reviews in one afternoon.

A schedule of one, three, seven and fourteen days after reading is a convenient plan, and nothing about those numbers is magic: what matters is that the gaps grow. Suppose you read on 5 November. Counting forward gives reviews on 6, 8, 12 and 19 November, and each review can be five minutes of trying to recall the chapter and then checking it.

lead.text: Once a week, choose one book you are reading and tell someone, or tell the room, what it argues so far and what you have not yet understood. You are retrieving the large shape of the book, and you will notice at once which parts you cannot say.

This also settles what to do when a review shows you have forgotten something. Go back to the page, read the passage again, and then put the book away and try again a few days later. Rereading then has a purpose, because you are rereading what you could not recall and are not rereading from habit.

blocks.text: Think of a chapter you read carefully a week or two ago. While you were reading it, it was clear, and if you opened it now it would probably still feel familiar, since the page would look just as it did. Yet if you closed the book and tried to say what the chapter argued, many of us would struggle to give more than a sentence or two of something that took an hour to read.
Familiar and remembered are different states, and treating them as one is how a reader keeps finishing books they cannot describe.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to use recall after reading, explain why a familiar page misleads, and set a schedule of reviews.
intro.whyItMatters: Reading takes the hours, and these methods make sure the hours leave something behind.

recap.keyIdea: Recall what you read with the page closed, and repeat that recall at growing gaps, because a familiar page feels like knowledge when it is not.

blocks.text: Retrieval practice strengthens memory more than rereading, because producing an answer builds the route to it and shows you where the gaps are. The fluency illusion makes a familiar page feel like knowledge, so spacing your reviews, for example after 1, 3, 7 and 14 days, is the way to keep it.

lessons.title: Kinds of source

lead.text: Imagine a town council voted to close a swimming pool. The minutes of the meeting, a resident's letter to the council, and the usage figures the council had in front of it all come from the events themselves. A newspaper article analysing why the council decided as it did comes next, and a local-history book that summarises the decade's decisions comes after that.

A **primary source** is direct evidence, made by participants or from original observation or data: an interview transcript, a diary, a table of official figures. A **secondary source** analyses primary sources, as a review article or most news features do. A **tertiary source** summarises secondary sources, which is what a textbook or an encyclopaedia entry does.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the words describe a relation, not a format, so one document can play more than one role, depending on what you use it as evidence of.

lead.text: Take six items and sort them. An interview transcript is primary, since it records what someone said. A journal article reporting a new experiment is primary for that experiment, and a government data table is primary data. A review article that analyses the published studies on a question is secondary, and so is a newspaper feature that reports and interprets research. A textbook, summarising what the field accepts, is tertiary.

Then ask what each kind is good for. Primary sources give you the evidence itself, which is what you want when you must check a claim. Secondary sources give you someone's analysis, which saves you the work of reading a hundred studies. Tertiary sources give you the shape of a field in an afternoon, but they are the end of nobody's research: an encyclopaedia entry is where you begin, and its bibliography is where you go next.

lead.text: Where do journal articles come from, and why do we trust them more than a blog post? Most scholarly journals send a submitted paper to other experts in the field, who judge whether its methods and reasoning are sound enough to publish. That process is **peer review**, and it is a real filter, because papers get rejected or revised on the strength of what the reviewers say.

But it is a filter and not a guarantee. Reviewers read the paper and rarely repeat the work, so they can miss errors, and a paper that passes can still be wrong. Findings are sometimes shared before review as a **preprint**, which lets others see results early but means no reviewer has yet judged them. And when a mistake or misconduct is found after publication, the journal can issue a **retraction**, withdrawing the paper with a notice that explains why. A **scholarly** source is written by experts for experts, a **popular** one for general readers, and a **trade** source for people working in an industry, and none of the three is reliable or unreliable by label alone.

reveal.text: The answer fits the process: reviewers judge a manuscript, and few of them have the means to repeat the work.

steps.headline: Choose a kind of source for each need: an overview of an unfamiliar field, evidence for a claim, and this year's published figures.

workedSteps.text: An overview wants someone else to have done the summarising already, so look for a tertiary source such as a textbook chapter or an encyclopaedia entry.
Evidence for a claim wants the nearest source to the evidence, so look for the primary study, or for a review article that analyses several of them.
The last need is this year's published figures, which a summary written last year cannot contain.

lead.text: Where do you actually find these things? A library catalogue and its databases are the first stop, but some journals publish their articles free to read, and the Directory of Open Access Journals, or DOAJ, is an index of such journals.

Whatever you find, treat the reference list at its end as a map. A tertiary source points to the secondary ones it summarised, and those in turn point to the primary studies, so you can start with an encyclopaedia and, a few steps later, be holding the evidence.

reveal.text: For the experiment it reports, a preprint is a primary source. Read it for what it shows, check whether a reviewed version has appeared, and lean on it only as far as its design justifies.
The way to the figure runs back through the feature's source, which is why a feature that names its study is worth more than one that does not.

lessons.orientation: Classify sources as primary, secondary or tertiary and choose one for a need.
lessons.nextAction: Apply lateral reading and the SIFT moves to an unfamiliar source and decide how far to trust it.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to know whether a new drug works, and you find five documents: a news article headed "Drug cuts risk by half", the journal paper it was based on, a textbook chapter on the drug's class, a review article comparing it with older treatments, and the trial's published data tables. All five are about the same drug, yet they are not the same kind of evidence, and reading them as if they were is how people come away believing a headline.

What separates them is how many steps each one stands from the trial itself. The data tables record what was measured, the news article retells someone else's account of it, and the others sit at different distances in between.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sort a source as primary, secondary or tertiary, say what peer review does and does not do, and pick a source for a need.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing where a document sits relative to the evidence tells you what you can safely take from it.

recap.keyIdea: A source is primary, secondary or tertiary by how close it stands to the evidence, and each kind suits a different need.

blocks.text: Primary sources are the evidence itself, secondary sources analyse it, and tertiary sources summarise the analyses. Peer review improves a paper's odds without guaranteeing it, and preprints and retractions show that publication is a stage in a paper's life, not the end of it.

recap.nextHook: Next we meet a source with no label at all, a website from an organisation you have never heard of, and learn how to judge it.

lessons.title: Judging a source

lead.text: Imagine a site called the Institute for Healthy Living, which we have invented for this lesson. It has a clean layout, an article headed "New study shows supplement X improves memory", a named author, a recent date and an About page that calls it "a trusted voice since 2009". Would you trust it? Most of us feel inclined to, and a checklist of features such as author, date, design and About page would also pass it.

A **checklist** like that is easy to apply, and that is both its attraction and its weakness. Every item on it is something a site can supply for itself, so a careful-looking page that exists to sell a supplement scores as well as an honest one. A checklist cannot tell you who is behind the page, because the page is the only thing it looks at.

reveal.text: The page can only tell you what its makers want to say, so the answer is to go and ask someone else.

lead.text: How do people who are good at judging websites actually do it? Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew put the question to 45 people: ten PhD historians, ten professional fact-checkers and twenty-five Stanford undergraduates, reported in *Teachers College Record* in 2019. The historians and the students tended to stay on the unfamiliar site and read it closely, scrolling the page and studying its About section, but the fact-checkers did something different. They left the site within moments, opened new tabs, and searched for the organisation and its claims.

That habit is called **lateral reading**, since you move across the web and not down the page. It works because a site cannot control what the rest of the web says about it. The fact-checkers arrived at better judgements by reading less of the site and more about it.

reveal.text: Your judgement now draws on sources the site did not write, which is where reliable evidence about it has to come from.

lead.text: Lateral reading is a habit, and Mike Caulfield turned it into a routine he called SIFT, published in 2019. **Stop** is first: before you read, ask whether you know the source and how far it deserves your effort. **Investigate the source** is next, which means finding out who made the page and what their record is, usually in a new tab.

**Find better coverage** asks what other sources say about the claim, since a claim worth believing will be reported somewhere you can judge. **Trace** goes to the original of a claim, quote or image, to see what it said and in what context before it was passed on.

reveal.text: The order follows an economy of effort: a few seconds on the first, a minute or two on the next, and the longest work only for a claim you have decided to chase.

steps.headline: Apply SIFT to the invented Institute for Healthy Living and its supplement article.

workedSteps.text: Stop. You have never heard of the Institute, so you know nothing about it yet, and the page looks professional, which proves nothing.
The Institute's own pages can only say what the Institute wants said, so you leave the page and open a new tab.
Suppose the results show that the Institute is funded by the maker of supplement X. That is a reason to treat its article as advertising for that supplement.
Find better coverage of the claim from sources with no stake in it, and trace the cited study to see what it found.

lead.text: After the moves you still have to decide. You may trust a source fully on a question, because you have found it has a good record and no stake in the answer. You may trust it for some things, such as a company's description of its own product's size or price, while treating its claims about what the product does as unproven. Or you may decide not to rely on it, and use it only as a lead to better sources.
Notice that the decision attaches to a question and a source together, not to the source alone. The same organisation can be reliable about its own members and unreliable about a medical claim.

steps.headline: A page says "studies show that supplement X improves memory". Decide what to check.

workedSteps.text: The claim names no study, so Stop and ask who made it: the Institute, which sells supplement X.
Find better coverage by searching for reports of supplement X with no connection to its seller.
One thing is still unchecked: the claim itself.

reveal.text: Evidence about a source has to come from somewhere other than the source, and that is why you look beyond the About page.

lessons.orientation: Use lateral reading and the SIFT moves to judge an unfamiliar source.
lessons.nextAction: Tell relative from absolute change and match a claim to the design of the study behind it.

blocks.text: Everything you can see on a web page was put there by whoever made it: the design, the author's name, the date and the About page that says who they are. So when we judge a page by those features, as most of us were taught to, we are judging it by evidence its own author chose, and a site that exists to sell something can supply all of it as easily as an honest one.

Does that leave you with no way to judge a source you have never met? It doesn't, because the people who check sources for a living use a quick method that works on any site and takes a minute or two.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read an unfamiliar source laterally, put the four SIFT moves in order and decide how far to trust it.
intro.whyItMatters: Anyone can make a page look careful, so the useful evidence about a source lies off the page.

recap.keyIdea: Before you read an unfamiliar page closely, leave it and find out who is behind it, using Stop, Investigate, Find better coverage and Trace.

blocks.text: A checklist looks at features a site supplies for itself, so it cannot tell you who stands behind the site. Lateral reading, which fact-checkers practise in the Wineburg and McGrew study, leaves the page to find out, and the four SIFT moves give that habit an order.

lessons.title: Judging a claim and its numbers

reveal.text: One person in a thousand is the entire benefit, and the next screen gives names to the different ways of reporting that single fact.

lead.text: A headline reads: "New drug halves the risk of a rare event". It sounds like a great deal, and you could be forgiven for picturing a large number of people spared. Suppose the risk was 2 in 1,000 without the drug and is 1 in 1,000 with it. Halving describes that change correctly, yet in a group of a thousand people exactly one person is spared.

Compare a second drug that cuts the risk of a common event from 20 in 100 to 10 in 100. It also halves the risk, but now ten people in every hundred are spared. The headlines would read the same, while the two effects differ a hundredfold.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, the first view shows the rare case where each square stands for ten people and the event fills a sliver of a single square. The second shows the common case, where each square is one person and a tenth of the grid changes.

diagram.alt: Two before-and-after grids of 100 squares. In the rare case each square stands for 10 people and the event fills a sliver of one square before and half that sliver after. In the common case each square is one person, with 20 filled before and 10 after.
diagram.caption: Both treatments halve the risk. Use the buttons to see how different the change is to the people involved.

steps.headline: Three ways to report an effect

lead.text: A change in risk can be told in three ways, and a careful reader asks for all of them. The **relative reduction** compares the fall to the old rate: the fall divided by the old risk, here 1 in 1,000 against 2 in 1,000, which is 50%. The **absolute reduction** is the plain difference between the two rates, and here it is 0.2% minus 0.1%, or 0.1 percentage points. The **number needed to treat** is how many people must receive the treatment for one of them to benefit, and it is 1 divided by the absolute reduction written as a proportion: 1 ÷ 0.001 = 1,000.

Which one should you trust? None of them is false, but only the relative reduction can be made to sound large when the effect is small, so the absolute reduction and the number needed to treat are the ones that tell you what happens to a person. Notice also that percentage points are the unit for a difference between two percentages, so 0.1 percentage points is not 0.1%.

diagram.alt: One effect worked out three ways. A risk falls from 0.2% to 0.1%; the relative reduction is 50%, the absolute reduction is 0.1 percentage points, and the number needed to treat is 1,000.

steps.headline: Work out the relative reduction, absolute reduction and number needed to treat when risk falls from 8 in 1,000 to 6 in 1,000.

workedSteps.text: Write both rates as percentages so they can be compared: 8 in 1,000 is 0.8%, and 6 in 1,000 is 0.6%.
The relative reduction is the fall divided by the old rate.
The absolute reduction is the plain difference, and it is a difference of percentages, so the unit is percentage points.
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute reduction as a proportion, which is 0.002.

steps.headline: Work out the three numbers when risk falls from 40 in 100 to 20 in 100.

workedSteps.text: As percentages the rates are 40% and 20%, so the relative reduction is the fall of 20 over the old rate of 40.
The absolute reduction is the plain difference, 20 percentage points, which as a proportion is 0.20.
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by that proportion.

lead.text: In an **experiment** the researchers decide who gets the exposure, assigning people to groups by chance, so that other differences, whether in age, health or habit, are spread evenly. In an **observational study** they only record what people already do. If the groups differ in some other way that matters, a [[confound|A third factor that produces an association between two other things. Met in the logic and statistics courses.]], the numbers will show an association that has nothing to do with the exposure.

So a headline's verb deserves attention. "Lowers", "causes" and "prevents" are claims about cause, and they need a design that can bear them. "Is linked to", "is associated with" and "goes with" are claims about association, and an observational study can support those.

reveal.text: The survey recorded habits and assigned none, so the claim it can support is the weaker one, which is the point of matching a claim to its design.

lead.text: Two more checks help. The first is the sample: who was in the study, how many of them were there, and are they like the people the headline is about? A result from 40 volunteers at one university tells you little about the whole population, and a result in adults may not carry over to children. The second concerns the decimals. A figure such as 12.347% looks careful, yet it comes from the same few people as 12%, so the extra digits give you an impression of precision rather than any more evidence.
None of this means a number should be dismissed. It means asking what the number measures, in whom, and by what design, and then saying in a sentence the claim the study can actually carry.

reveal.text: The relative reduction here is the same size as many headline figures, though the change is one person in a hundred. Asking for the absolute reduction is what shows it.

lessons.orientation: Tell relative from absolute change, compute a number needed to treat and match a claim to a design.

lessons.nextAction: Build a search from a question using synonyms, Boolean operators and filters, and extend it by following citations.

blocks.text: A headline that says a new drug "halves the risk" can be perfectly accurate and still leave you unable to say whether the drug matters. Halving a risk of 20 in 100 and halving a risk of 2 in 1,000 are both described by that one word, yet for a person deciding whether to take the drug they are very different results.

What the headline leaves out is how large the risk was before, and once you have that number you can turn the claim into figures that describe what happens to people: how many fewer of them have the event, and how many must be treated for one to benefit.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to turn a relative claim into an absolute one, work out a number needed to treat, and match a claim to its study design.
intro.whyItMatters: Headlines report the biggest-sounding version of a result, and the numbers underneath say how large it is.

recap.keyIdea: Ask for the absolute change and the number needed to treat as well as the relative one, and check that the study's design can bear the claim made.

blocks.text: A relative reduction compares a fall to the old rate, an absolute reduction is the plain difference, and the number needed to treat is 1 divided by that difference as a proportion. Together with the design of the study, and who was in it, they say whether a headline's verb is earned.

lessons.title: Searching well

reveal.text: Each concept gets its own group of words, and the next screen says how the groups are joined, with the three operators that Boolean searching offers.

lead.text: You have a question: how does school start time affect teenagers' sleep? The natural move is to type it in as a sentence and read the first page of results, and it is worth seeing why that disappoints. A search engine matches words, and the papers you want may say "adolescents" where you said "teenagers", or "sleep duration" where you said "sleep".

A better habit is to take the question apart. It has three concepts: teenagers, sleep and school start time. For each, list the other words researchers might use, such as adolescents for teenagers. The words for one concept go together, because any one of them will do, and the three concepts go together in a different way, because the paper must be about all three.

lead.text: Searching with these joiners is named for George Boole, the nineteenth-century logician. Think of search A as a set of results, search B as another, and some results as belonging to both. **AND** returns only the results in both sets, so it narrows. **OR** returns everything in either, so it widens. **NOT** removes from the first set whatever is also in the second.

Why does that matter for the query? Because joining synonyms with AND is a mistake that narrows a search to almost nothing: "teen AND adolescent" asks for papers that use both words, when what you want is papers that use either. Use OR inside a concept and AND between concepts. Notice also that NOT is a blunt tool, since it deletes every record that mentions the excluded word, including the useful ones.

OR returns what is in either set. Adding 100 and 80 counts the 30 shared results twice.
NOT removes the shared results from A.

steps.headline: Work out the counts when A has 70 results, B has 45 and 15 are in both.

workedSteps.text: A AND B is the overlap.
A OR B counts the overlap once.
A NOT B keeps the results in A that are not in B.

lead.text: Quotation marks around words, as in "school start time", ask for the words together in that order, so that a paper that merely mentions schools, starting and time elsewhere is not returned. An asterisk after a stem, as in educat*, matches education, educator and educated at once, and this is called **truncation**. The symbol varies, and some databases use a question mark or a dollar sign, so check the help page of the one you are using.

A stem can be cut too short: art* matches artist and article and artillery along with the art you wanted, so truncate where the stem is specific. After the search, the filters the database offers, such as date, subject or peer-reviewed articles only, narrow what you have found.

reveal.text: Truncation saves you listing every ending, and it needs a stem long enough to keep unrelated words out.

lead.text: Even a well-built search misses things, because not everything uses your words. The remedy is to follow the literature itself. Take a good source and look at its reference list, which leads backward to the earlier work it relied on. Then look at the papers that cite it, which a service such as Google Scholar shows as a "Cited by" link and which leads forward to later work. Following references in these two directions is called **citation chaining**.

The search finds you the first good paper and the chain finds the ones that share its concerns whatever words they use, and when new searches and chains keep returning papers you have already seen, you have probably found what exists.

reveal.text: Chaining gives you a trail that no choice of search words could, because it follows the authors' own connections.
Reversing the order changed the answer, since NOT always removes the second set from the first.

lessons.orientation: Build a query with synonyms and Boolean operators, count what each returns and follow citations.
lessons.nextAction: Write quotation, paraphrase, summary and comment notes with their sources, and tell a paraphrase from a copy.

blocks.text: Type "how does school start time affect teenagers' sleep" into a search box and you will get pages of results, most of them nearly right. Yet the papers that answer the question best may never contain the word "teenagers", because the researchers wrote "adolescents", and no amount of scrolling will show you what the search did not match.
Search engines and library databases match the words you give them and little else, so finding what exists depends on choosing those words and on telling the database how they combine.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to turn a question into a query with OR and AND, work out how many results each operator returns, and extend a search by following citations.
intro.whyItMatters: A search that misses the key papers makes every later step less reliable.

recap.keyIdea: Pull the concepts from the question, join the synonyms of each with OR and the concepts with AND, then follow citations from the best sources you find.

blocks.text: A query groups the words for each concept with OR and joins the concepts with AND, and quotation marks and truncation make it exact. OR counts shared results once, so A OR B is A plus B minus the overlap, and citation chaining finds papers that no choice of words would.

lessons.title: Notes you can use later

lead.text: Suppose you copy a sentence from an article into your notes and, a month later, find it there with no mark on it. Is it yours, or theirs? You cannot tell, and neither could anyone who read your work, which is how a plain tired afternoon of note-taking turns into an accidental case of plagiarism. The remedy is to decide, for each note, what kind it is, and to write that down.

There are four kinds worth having. A **quotation** gives the exact words, in quotation marks, with the page. A **paraphrase** restates one passage's idea in your own words and your own structure, and it is still cited, because the idea is the source's. A **summary** shortens a whole source or section to its main points, in your own words. A **comment** is your own reaction, kept apart from what the source says. Every note except a comment also carries its source: author, year and the page.

reveal.text: Whether a rewrite is yours depends on whether you changed how the idea is built, and not on how many words you swapped. The next screen gives the name for the one that did not.

lead.text: Look at the two rewrites in the figure. The first changes "grown" to "raised", "stretch" to "grow" and "those" to "ones", and otherwise follows the original phrase for phrase. The second says that plants kept in dim conditions reach for the glass sooner than brightly lit plants do. Which one would you say is yours?

The first is **patchwriting**: the original with a few patches of new words, still in its structure and its order. It is not a paraphrase, even though every word looks different on a quick glance, and putting it in your notes unmarked is the same mistake as copying. A true paraphrase means understanding the idea and rebuilding it, and a reliable test is to write it with the source closed. Even then, the idea is the source's, so the paraphrase is cited.

reveal.text: Telling a paraphrase from a patch is the main skill of this lesson, and the closed-book test is the practical way to do it.

lead.text: Why does the source line matter so much? Because a note without one cannot be cited, and finding the source again weeks later is slow and sometimes impossible. Write author, year and page at the moment you write the note, even if the note is only a few words, and for a web page note the address and the date you read it.

Keep your comments apart too. A line such as "does this hold for older plants?" belongs in a separate comment note or a separate field, because mixed in with the source's claims it will one day be mistaken for something the source said.

reveal.text: The marks cost nothing at the time and remove the doubt a month later, which is the point of a note that you can reuse.

steps.headline: Make a note from the seedling sentence, taken from an invented source, Lee 2019, page 14.

workedSteps.text: Decide what you need. If the exact wording matters, quote it, and copy it exactly inside quotation marks: "Seedlings grown in low light stretch toward the window faster than those grown in bright light."

If only the idea matters, close the source and write the idea from memory, with a new structure, and then check it against the source: Plants kept in dim conditions reach for the glass sooner than brightly lit plants do.
The second note is in your own words and your own structure, and it covers a single passage.
Add the source line to every note.

lead.text: Notes that only copy what a source says are a poor substitute for the source. Their worth comes from what you add: a question you want to answer, a link to another source, a doubt about the method. Each of these goes in a comment, and the comment is the part of the note that will start your own writing.
A useful habit is to end each note with one comment, even a short one. It forces you to decide, while the passage is in front of you, what you think it is for.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence from an article: "Seedlings grown in low light stretch toward the window faster than those grown in bright light." If you copy it into your notes without quotation marks, in a month it will look exactly like something you wrote, and if you change a few of its words to make it look different, it will look even more like your own.
Either way the note has stopped telling you whose words and whose idea it holds, which is how honest note-taking turns into plagiarism without anyone intending it.

recap.keyIdea: Give every note a type and a source, put exact words in quotation marks, and rebuild an idea in your own structure before you call it a paraphrase.

blocks.text: A note is a quotation, a paraphrase, a summary or a comment, and every note except a comment carries its author, year and page. Patchwriting, which swaps a few words but keeps the original's structure, is not a paraphrase, so exact words need quotation marks and a real paraphrase needs a new structure.

recap.nextHook: Next we put several sources together in a matrix and write a synthesis that says more than any one of them.

lessons.title: Combining sources

reveal.text: Putting sources in order is a start, and the next screens show a tool for doing the comparing.

lead.text: Suppose you have read three papers on the same question and are about to write about them. The easiest plan is to give each paper a paragraph: Source A found this, Source B found that, Source C found something else. It is accurate, and it is a summary of each source in turn. What it does not do is say how they fit together, and the reader is left to notice that B contradicts A, or that C answers a question the other two left open.

A **synthesis** is a new statement built from several sources and organised by ideas, not by source. Each paragraph takes one idea, such as whether the treatment works, and draws on every source that has something to say about it, saying where they agree, where they conflict and what none of them covers. Hiding a conflict to make the sources sound as though they agree is the failure to avoid.

lead.text: How do you see the whole of a set of sources at once? Put them in a table. A **matrix** has one row for each source and one column for each question you want to ask of every source, such as how many participants, what the design was and what was found. Filling it in forces you to ask the same questions of every source, and the gaps in the table show you what a source never said.

Then read in two directions. Reading down a column shows how the sources compare on one question, and reading across a row tells you the shape of one source. Here we use five studies of a treatment that we have invented for the lesson, with 400, 250, 120, 2,000 and 90 participants, of which the first three found a benefit, the fourth found none and the last found harm.

workedSteps.text: The participants are 300, 150, 80, 1,200 and 70. Add the three benefit studies first.

lead.text: Now compare what the table says with what a quick count says. Three of the five studies found a benefit, which is 60% of them, and it is tempting to call the case for a benefit stronger than not. Yet the three benefit studies have only 770 of the 2,860 participants, about 27%, and the one study that found no benefit has 2,000 on its own. Judging a question by how many studies agree, and ignoring the size of each, is called **vote counting**, and here it overstates the support.

Why should size matter? A small study is more easily moved by chance, so a result in 90 people is a weaker guide than one in 2,000. Size is only a rough guide, though: a large study with a poor design can mislead, and a careful small one can be sound. So we weigh sources by size, by design and by how closely they fit your question, and say in the synthesis why we trusted some more than others.

lead.text: To write one, follow four moves. State your **claim** about what the sources show together. Give the **support**, naming the sources and saying how strong each is. Describe the **conflict**, saying which sources disagree and why you weight them as you do. Finish with the **gap**: what the sources do not settle.

For the invented studies a paragraph might run: the treatment may help, since three studies with 770 participants found a benefit, but the largest study, with 2,000 participants, found none, and the smallest, with 90, found harm. Because most participants were in studies that did not find a benefit, the case for it is weak, and a larger study with a stricter design is what is needed.

reveal.text: Here the weight sits with the single large study, the reverse of the five studies in the matrix, and in both cases a synthesis has to say how it weighed the sources and why.

blocks.text: Suppose five studies have tested a treatment, and three of them found a benefit, one found nothing and one found harm. Counted by a show of hands the treatment wins three to two, and a quick summary would say that most studies support it, but once you look at how many people took part in each study that verdict becomes much harder to defend.
Most questions worth asking have several sources like these, and they rarely agree.

lessons.title: Citing so a reader can follow

reveal.text: The one that comes from a particular study is the one that needs its source named, because only the source can confirm it.

lead.text: Why cite at all? A citation does two jobs. It lets a reader go and check what you say, and it gives credit to the person whose work you used. Both are lost if the citation is missing, which is why the usual list of what needs one is longer than people expect: not only direct quotations, but paraphrases, data and any idea that is distinctive to a particular author.

What does not need one is **common knowledge**: a fact widely known and easily found in many sources, such as that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level. A useful test is to ask whether a reader could find the claim in many places or only in one. A statistic from a particular survey is found in one, since it belongs to that survey, and so it needs the citation. The test depends on the reader, so when in doubt, cite.

lead.text: What does a reader need in order to find an article? The reference supplies it in parts: the author, the year, the title of the article, the **container** it sits in, which for an article is the journal, and the volume, issue and pages of that journal. Most also end with a **DOI**, a persistent identifier that resolves to the published work, and so goes on working when a publisher redesigns its website.

The author and year say whose work and which version, the title and journal say what and where, and the volume and pages say where to turn. The example is invented, and its DOI will not resolve. When a part is missing the reference still looks like one, which is why you have to check parts and not just the look.

steps.headline: Read the invented reference: Lee, J. (2019). Light and seedling growth. Journal of Plant Studies, 12(3), 14-29.

workedSteps.text: The author is Lee, J., and the year, in brackets, is 2019, which tells you whose work this is and when.
The next piece is the title of the article, Light and seedling growth.
After the title comes Journal of Plant Studies.
Last come the volume, 12, the issue, 3, in brackets, and the pages, 14 to 29.

lead.text: If every reference holds the same parts, why do citation styles differ? Because each style, such as APA, MLA or Chicago, orders and punctuates the same parts in its own way, as the third view of the reference figure earlier in the lesson showed. Some put the year in brackets after the author, others put it near the end, and which a field uses is a matter of its convention.
Within a single piece of writing the choice is not a matter of taste. One style used consistently lets a reader learn the pattern once and then read your list at a glance.

The volume and issue are given as 12(3), so a reader knows which issue of the journal to look in.
A reader holding that issue still cannot turn to the article.

lead.text: References are easy to get wrong in ways that look fine. A typing slip in a DOI points to nothing, a year is off by one, and a tool that formats your list will format whatever you gave it. Reference managers such as Zotero save a great deal of typing and keep the parts in fields, but they do not read the paper for you, so each entry still needs a look.

The newest risk is a reference you did not write yourself. An AI tool asked for sources can produce a reference with a plausible author, title and journal for a paper that does not exist. Treat any reference you cannot find in a database as **unverified** and leave it out until you have located the work. A good habit is to open each cited source at least once, and to check that it says what you say it says.
