A conclusion sums up the argument and seldom carries the date of one factory, so the reading would end without the fact.
That would find the year, but at the price of an hour for a fact that sits in a few lines. The purpose is a single fact, so the pass can be much lighter.

questions.prompt: The quick first pass over a text's title, abstract, headings, conclusion and figures, made before reading closely, is called a what?
hints: It names the first step of a routine you meet on the next screens.
Think of looking over the ground before you walk across it.
questions.onCorrect: A survey takes a few minutes and tells you the shape of the text, which is what lets you decide how much of it to read.

questions.prompt: A 12,000-word article, read at 240 words per minute, takes how many minutes?
hints: Time is length divided by speed.
Divide 12,000 words by the number of words you read each minute.
12,000 divided by 240 is the number of minutes.
questions.onCorrect: At 240 words a minute, 12,000 words take 50 minutes, which is the figure to plan around if you mean to read it straight through.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. Time is length divided by speed.
Check the division again: 240 goes into 12,000 fifty times.

questions.prompt: You plan to read a 300-page book at 25 pages a day. How many days will it take?
hints: Pages in the book divided by pages per day gives days.
How many lots of 25 fit into 300?
25 times 10 is 250, so you need a little more than ten days.
questions.onCorrect: The same division works for any pace, so it turns a book into a calendar: 300 pages at 25 a day is 12 days.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies. Days are pages divided by pages per day.

questions.prompt: A report has 9,600 words. Your survey shows that only its last 2,400 words matter to your question. At 240 words per minute, how many minutes does reading just that part take?
hints: Estimate only the part you will read.
The words that matter are 2,400.
2,400 divided by 240.
questions.onCorrect: Surveying first turned a 40-minute read into a 10-minute one, which is the saving the survey exists to find.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2,400 ÷ 240 = 10 minutes, against 9,600 ÷ 240 = 40 minutes for the whole report.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time for the whole report. The question asks only about the last 2,400 words.

questions.prompt: Which order do the five steps of SQ3R come in?
hints: The name spells the order.
Each letter is a step, and the 3 R's come last.
questions.onCorrect: The letters of SQ3R are the steps in order, with the questions deliberately placed before the reading.

choices.label: Read, Recite, Review, Survey, Question
Survey, Read, Question, Recite, Review
Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review
Question, Survey, Read, Review, Recite

misconceptions.feedback: Surveying comes first, because you need to see what the text covers before you can ask sensible questions about it.
Reading is the third step. Before it come the survey, which shows the shape, and the questions, which give you something to read for.
The questions come before the reading, since they are what you read to answer.

questions.prompt: An 18,000-word report is read at 240 words per minute. How many minutes will it take?
hints: Length divided by speed.
18,000 divided by 240.
questions.onCorrect: Seventy-five minutes is an hour and a quarter, long enough that surveying first to decide what to read is worth the few minutes it costs.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the division. 240 × 75 = 18,000.

questions.prompt: A 420-page book is read at 35 pages a day. How many days will it take?
hints: Pages divided by pages per day.
35 times 10 is 350.
Another two lots of 35 make 420.
questions.onCorrect: A pace of 35 pages gets through the book in 12 days, so an even daily habit turns a large book into a fixed appointment.

questions.prompt: In SQ3R, what does the Q stand for?
hints: The second step comes after the survey and before the reading.
You turn the headings into something you want answered.
questions.onCorrect: Turning each heading into a question gives the reading a job to do, which is the reason this step comes before it.

questions.prompt: Read this: "Cities should plant more street trees. Shaded streets stay cooler in summer, so trees reduce heat-related illness." Which sentence is the claim, the statement the author wants you to accept?
hints: Ask what the author wants you to do or believe at the end.
A claim is the statement the other sentences are there to support.
questions.onCorrect: The claim is the sentence the others work for. Here both other sentences are offered to show that cities should plant more trees.

choices.label: Cities should plant more street trees
Shaded streets stay cooler in summer
Streets are often hot
Trees reduce heat-related illness

acceptedIdeas: Cities should plant more street trees
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cities should plant more street trees

misconceptions.feedback: That is a reason offered for the claim. It is something the author expects you to grant while you are being persuaded of something else.
That is a reason too, and it is introduced by the word "so", which marks it as following from the first reason. The claim is what the reasons are for.
The passage does not say that at all. It is not in the text, and the claim has to be something the author actually states.

questions.prompt: In Toulmin's layout, the evidence or reason offered in direct support of a claim is called its what?
hints: It is the first thing the author puts forward when asked "what have you got to go on?"
Toulmin used a word that also names the base of a building.
questions.onCorrect: Grounds are what the claim rests on, so a challenge to a claim is usually met by pointing to them.

questions.prompt: Claim: the town should run a bus to the hospital. Grounds: many patients miss appointments because they have no car. Which unstated assumption links the grounds to the claim?
hints: The grounds mention missed appointments, and the claim wants a bus. What fills the gap between them?
Which answer connects a bus to the problem the grounds describe?
questions.onCorrect: The author never says that patients without a car would take the bus to their appointments, yet the argument needs it, which is what makes it the warrant.

choices.label: A bus would get patients without a car to their appointments
Buses cost the town less than other ways of reaching the hospital
The hospital is too far from where most patients live to walk
Patients who miss their appointments end up with worse health

acceptedIdeas: A bus would get patients without a car to their appointments
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bus would get patients without a car to their appointments

misconceptions.feedback: Cost is a separate question. It does not connect missed appointments to a bus route.
That explains why having no car is a problem, but it does not say that a bus would solve it.
That may be so, but the argument still needs a step from a bus to fewer missed appointments, and this does not supply it.

questions.prompt: In the argument "Cities should plant more street trees, in hot climates", the phrase "in hot climates" limits the claim. What does Toulmin call a word or phrase like that?
hints: It qualifies how far the claim reaches.
The word begins with q.
questions.onCorrect: A qualifier marks how far the claim is meant to reach, and a claim that states its limits is easier to defend.

questions.prompt: "Unless trees' water use causes shortages" names a condition under which the street-trees claim would fail. Toulmin calls such a condition a what?
hints: It is a point that answers the argument rather than supports it.
It starts with r.
questions.onCorrect: A rebuttal names a case in which the claim would not hold, and saying it yourself shows you have thought about the argument.

questions.prompt: In "Shaded streets stay cooler, so trees reduce illness", which one word signals that a conclusion follows?
hints: Look for the small word between the two statements.
Such words are called indicator words, and this one is two letters long.
questions.onCorrect: Because, since and for introduce reasons, and so, therefore and thus introduce what follows from them.

questions.prompt: Claim: the school should serve breakfast. Grounds: many pupils arrive hungry. Which unstated assumption links the two?
hints: Ask what has to be true for hunger to count as a reason to serve breakfast.
Which answer joins the grounds to the claim?
questions.onCorrect: The argument needs hungry pupils to be helped by breakfast, and nothing in the passage says so, which is why it counts as an assumption.

choices.label: Schools have kitchens
Pupils like school
Breakfast is a meal
Hungry pupils learn less, and breakfast would fix that

acceptedIdeas: Hungry pupils learn less, and breakfast would fix that
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hungry pupils learn less, and breakfast would fix that

misconceptions.feedback: That is true of every breakfast, so it links nothing to the claim.
Whether a kitchen exists is a practical matter. It does not connect hunger to the reason for serving breakfast.
Whether pupils like school is outside the argument. The gap lies between hunger and the benefit of breakfast.

questions.prompt: In Toulmin's layout, what is the support offered for the warrant itself called?
hints: It stands behind the warrant, much as a person backs a claim.
It is not the grounds, which support the claim.
questions.onCorrect: Backing is evidence for the warrant, such as studies showing that cooler streets lead to fewer heat illnesses.

questions.prompt: The argument: the school should serve breakfast, because many pupils arrive hungry. The unstated step "hungry pupils learn less, and breakfast would help" plays which part in Toulmin's layout?
hints: It is neither the claim nor the evidence. It is the link between them.
Hungry pupils learn less is not stated in the passage.
questions.onCorrect: The warrant is the step the author needs you to grant, and here it is the one place the argument could be challenged with evidence about breakfast.

questions.prompt: You have just finished a chapter and have twenty minutes. Which use of them is most likely to help you recall it a week from now?
hints: Which option makes you produce something without the page in front of you?
Think about which one could leave you stuck.
questions.onCorrect: Retrieving from memory is hard in a way that rereading is not, and that difficulty is what strengthens the route back to the idea.

choices.label: Read the chapter again from the start
Copy the chapter headings into a list
Run a highlighter over the key sentences
Close the book and write what you remember

acceptedIdeas: Close the book and write what you remember
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Close the book and write what you remember

misconceptions.feedback: Rereading feels productive because the page is familiar, but familiarity is not recall. The next screens show why it falls behind.
Highlighting marks the page and leaves you with a page that looks organised, which is not the same as a memory that is.
Copying headings is copying, and it asks nothing of your memory. The useful step is the one where you have to produce something from nothing.

questions.prompt: The feeling of knowing that comes from a familiar page, which does not show that you can recall its contents, is called the what?
hints: It is named after how smoothly the page reads.
Two words: the first is how easily something goes by.
questions.onCorrect: A page you recognise reads smoothly, and smoothness is easy to mistake for knowledge, which is why a test is a better judge of learning than a re-read.

questions.prompt: You read on 3 November and review after 3 days. Which date in November is that?
hints: Add the number of days to the date you read.
Count three days on from the 3rd.
questions.onCorrect: A review three days after the third of November is on the sixth, the second review in the 1, 3, 7 and 14 day plan.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the day you read. Add the 3 days to it.

questions.prompt: You read on 12 November and use reviews after 1, 3, 7 and 14 days. On which November date is the last review?
hints: The last review is the 14-day one.
Add 14 to the date you read.
questions.onCorrect: Fourteen days after the twelfth of November is the twenty-sixth, and the earlier reviews fall on the 13th, 15th and 19th.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 7-day review. The last one is 14 days after reading.

questions.prompt: You read on 27 November and want a review 7 days later. On which day of December does it fall? November has 30 days.
hints: 27 + 7 goes past the end of the month.
27 + 7 = 34, and November has 30 days.
Subtract the 30 days of November from 34.
questions.onCorrect: Counting past the end of the month, 27 + 7 = 34 and 34 − 30 = 4, so the review is on 4 December.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the date before it rolls over. November ends on the 30th, so count on into December.

questions.prompt: You read on 8 November and review after 7 days. Which November date is that?
hints: Add 7 to the date.
Count seven days on from the 8th.
questions.onCorrect: A week after the eighth is the fifteenth, which stays in November because 15 is well under 30.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the interval. Add it to the date you read, which is the 8th.

questions.prompt: You read on 20 November and review after 14 days. On which day of December is that? November has 30 days.
hints: 20 + 14 goes past the end of November.
Take 30 days of November from 34.
questions.onCorrect: The fortnight carries you past the end of November, so 20 + 14 = 34 and 34 − 30 = 4 December.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count before the month changes. Subtract the 30 days of November.

questions.prompt: Spreading reviews over days and weeks, and not massing them into one session, is called what?
hints: It is about the gaps between sessions.
The word starts with "space".
questions.onCorrect: Spacing gives you time to forget a little between reviews, so each retrieval is harder and does more for memory than another pass in the same sitting.

questions.prompt: A journal article reports an experiment that its own authors ran. For that experiment, what kind of source is the article?
hints: Who produced the evidence: the authors, or someone describing it?
questions.onCorrect: The authors are the ones who made the observations, so for that experiment the article is a primary source, however much else it also quotes.

acceptedIdeas: Primary, because the authors made the observations themselves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Primary, because the authors made the observations themselves

choices.label: Secondary, because it appears in a journal, and journals report on research
Tertiary, because the article was written up after the work was finished
Primary, because the authors made the observations themselves

misconceptions.feedback: Where an article is published doesn't decide its kind. What matters is that its authors made the observations themselves, which puts it right at the evidence.
Every source is written after the events it records. A tertiary source summarises other people's analyses, while this article reports observations its own authors made.

questions.prompt: A biography of a scientist analyses her letters and lab notebooks to explain her work. What kind of source is the biography?
hints: Ask how far the biography stands from the evidence.
What did the biographer work from: the evidence itself, or other people's analyses?
questions.onCorrect: The biography analyses papers its subject wrote, so it sits one step from the evidence, which is what makes it secondary. The letters and notebooks themselves are primary.

choices.label: Primary
Secondary
Tertiary

misconceptions.feedback: The letters and notebooks are the primary sources here. The biography is a later account that works from them.
A tertiary source sums up analyses that other people have already made, as a textbook does. The biography goes back to the letters and notebooks themselves.

questions.prompt: An article has passed peer review. What does that tell you?
hints: What have the reviewers actually done, and what could they not do?
Think about whether reviewers rerun the experiments.
questions.onCorrect: Peer review is a filter and not a guarantee, which is why a reviewed paper can still be corrected or later withdrawn.

choices.label: Its conclusions are correct, since a panel of experts approved it
It is a primary source, since experts have vouched for it
Its authors had no financial interest in the result
Experts judged it fit to publish, and it may still hold errors

acceptedIdeas: Experts judged it fit to publish, and it may still hold errors
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Experts judged it fit to publish, and it may still hold errors

misconceptions.feedback: Reviewers read the manuscript and the claims, but they usually cannot repeat the work, so a paper can pass and still be wrong. Errors found later can lead to a correction or a retraction.
Peer review is a check on quality, whereas a primary source is a matter of how close the document is to the evidence. A reviewed article can be primary or secondary.
Reviewers judge methods and reasoning and may not check who paid for the work, so peer review is not a test for bias of this kind.

questions.prompt: You need this year's published unemployment figures. A government statistics table of those counts is which kind of source: primary, secondary or tertiary?
hints: The table is the data itself, not an account of it.
Nobody has analysed it for you yet.
questions.onCorrect: A government data table is the primary evidence for a figure, and any summary of it is a step further away.

questions.prompt: A paper that authors make public before it has been through peer review is called a what?
hints: The name says it comes before the print version.
Servers such as arXiv hold them.
questions.onCorrect: A preprint lets readers see findings early, and since no reviewer has judged it yet, it deserves extra caution.

questions.prompt: A newspaper feature reports that "a new study shows that cities with more trees have fewer heat deaths". You need the study's actual figures. Where do you go?
hints: Where did the journalist get the figure?
Move toward the evidence, not away from it.
questions.onCorrect: To check a figure, go to where it came from. A feature that names its study gives you the way there.

choices.label: Read the feature again more slowly
Look up an encyclopaedia entry on trees
Find the study that the feature reports on
Search for other news stories on the same claim

acceptedIdeas: Find the study that the feature reports on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Find the study that the feature reports on

misconceptions.feedback: Rereading gets you the journalist's account again. The figures were chosen and summarised once already, and you want the version before that.
An encyclopaedia is a tertiary source, and it will not carry the figures from one particular recent study.
More stories mean more accounts of the same claim, each one a step further from the numbers.

questions.prompt: A textbook chapter summarises what is known about a field. What kind of source is it?
hints: Ask what a textbook is made from: observations, or other people's analyses?
questions.onCorrect: A textbook gathers the work of review articles and others into a summary, so it sits furthest from the evidence of the three kinds.

choices.label: Primary
Secondary
Tertiary

misconceptions.feedback: A primary source is the evidence itself, such as a transcript or a data table. A textbook describes a whole field and does not record any one observation.
A secondary source analyses primary sources, as a review article does. This one sums up analyses that other people have already made.

questions.prompt: You need a quick overview of a field you know nothing about. Which source should you start with?
hints: Which kind of source has already done the summarising for you?
You want the lie of the land, not the raw evidence.
questions.onCorrect: An encyclopaedia entry is a tertiary source, and a tertiary source sums up what others have analysed, so it is the quick way in. Its bibliography then points you onward.

choices.label: An encyclopaedia entry on the field
A preprint on one recent study
A raw dataset gathered in the field
An interview transcript with one expert

acceptedIdeas: An encyclopaedia entry on the field
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An encyclopaedia entry on the field

misconceptions.feedback: A preprint reports one set of findings and has not been reviewed, so it is a poor way to learn the lie of the land.
A dataset is evidence with nothing to tell you what it means, which is the opposite of an overview.
An interview gives one person's account at length, and it assumes you know the questions worth asking.

questions.prompt: When a journal formally withdraws a published paper because of an error or misconduct, it issues a what?
hints: The paper is taken back, and a notice says so.
The word begins with "retract".
questions.onCorrect: A retraction notice stays attached to the paper, so a reader who checks sees that it has been withdrawn and why.

questions.prompt: You land on an unfamiliar site with a polished design and an About page that sounds reputable. What is the best first move?
hints: What would a stranger say about the site if you asked them?
The site's own pages are written by the site.
questions.onCorrect: What others say about a site is harder for the site to control than its own pages, so the useful check is outside the page.

choices.label: Read the whole article carefully
Open a new tab and search for the site's name
Share it so others can judge
Check that the fonts and layout look professional

acceptedIdeas: Open a new tab and search for the site's name
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Open a new tab and search for the site's name

misconceptions.feedback: Reading closely first spends your attention on a page whose maker you know nothing about, and a persuasive page can be persuasive for any reason.
Design is the easiest thing about a site to buy or copy, so it says very little about who stands behind it.
Sharing is a way of vouching for the page before you have checked it, which is the thing you set out to do.

questions.prompt: Leaving a page to see what others say about its source, before reading the page closely, is called what? Two words.
hints: It is the opposite of reading vertically, down the page.
The first word is a direction sideways.
questions.onCorrect: Fact-checkers in the Stanford study left unfamiliar sites quickly and used new tabs, which is why the move is named after sideways travel across the web.

questions.prompt: Which order do the four SIFT moves come in?
hints: The name SIFT spells the order.
Each letter is one move.
questions.onCorrect: The letters give the order, and stopping first is deliberate, since it is the move that keeps you from reading on autopilot.

choices.label: Stop, Find better coverage, Investigate the source, Trace
Investigate the source, Stop, Trace, Find better coverage
Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace
Trace, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Stop

acceptedIdeas: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace

misconceptions.feedback: Stopping comes first, because you decide how much effort the page deserves before you give it any. Tracing comes last, since it needs the earlier moves to tell you which claim is worth chasing.
You learn who made the page before you look elsewhere for coverage, because knowing the source tells you what to look for in better coverage.
Tracing needs a claim you have decided is worth checking, and stopping comes at the start, not the end.

questions.prompt: In a new tab you search for the Institute's name, to find out who runs it and what its record is. Which SIFT move is this?
hints: Compare what each move asks: what you know, who made the page, what others say, or where a claim began.
questions.onCorrect: Investigating the source means asking who made the page and what their record is, and the answer usually lies off the page itself.

choices.label: Stop
Investigate the source
Find better coverage
Trace

misconceptions.feedback: Stop is the pause before you read, when you ask what you already know about the source. This search goes and finds out more.
Finding better coverage looks for what other sources say about the claim. This search is about who is behind the page.
Tracing goes back to the original of a claim, quote or image. Here no claim has been picked out yet, and the search is about the page's maker.

questions.prompt: A claim on a page cites "a study". Following it back to the study itself, to see what it says and whether it was quoted fairly, is which SIFT move? Answer with the first word of the move.
hints: It is the last move of the four.
The T in SIFT.
questions.onCorrect: Tracing takes you from the report of a claim to its origin, where you can see what was originally said and in what context.

questions.prompt: A site's own About page says it is a respected, independent organisation. How much does that page tell you about the site?
hints: Who wrote the About page?
Evidence about the site has to come from a different author.
questions.onCorrect: A site writes its own About page, so it is a claim the site makes about itself, and independent evidence has to come from elsewhere.

acceptedIdeas: Very little, since the site wrote that page about itself
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Very little, since the site wrote that page about itself

choices.label: Enough, provided the page names its staff and gives a founding date
Nothing at all, so the About page is not worth reading
Very little, since the site wrote that page about itself
A good deal, since a site would not risk saying something false about itself

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing stops a site from describing itself generously, and a site that exists to sell a supplement has every reason to. The page is the site's claim about itself, so it can't also be the check on that claim.
Names and dates are also things the site supplies for itself, which is the trouble with checklist features. They need confirming somewhere the site does not control.
The About page does tell you who the site says it is, which gives you a name to search for. It just can't confirm that description on its own.

questions.prompt: What does the S in SIFT stand for?
hints: The first move is not an action on the page.
It is the opposite of go.
questions.onCorrect: Stop is the first move because it asks what you already know about the source and how much it is worth checking.

questions.prompt: After checking, you find that the "Institute for Healthy Living" is funded by a company that sells the supplement it recommends. How far should you rely on its article about that supplement?
hints: Who benefits if you believe the article?
Decide the question the page is being used for, not the page as a whole.
questions.onCorrect: Trust is a decision about a question, and a source with a stake in the answer should not be your only evidence on it.

choices.label: Fully, because the page is professionally designed
Mostly, because a company would not mislead its own customers
Not by itself, because the seller gains if you believe it
Only as far as it cites a study, because that is evidence

acceptedIdeas: Not by itself, because the seller gains if you believe it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not by itself, because the seller gains if you believe it

misconceptions.feedback: Design is not evidence. A page can look careful while being written to sell something.
That takes the company's good faith for granted. A company that sells the supplement gains if you believe the article, so its word is not evidence.
A page that cites a study may have chosen it, quoted it selectively, or misread it. You still have to trace it.

questions.prompt: Which SIFT move leads you from a quoted statistic back to the original study it came from?
hints: Ask which move goes to the original and which move goes to other reports.
The move you want ends at the study and not at another account of it.
questions.onCorrect: Tracing a claim to its origin shows whether the original said what it was reported as saying.

choices.label: Stop
Investigate the source
Find better coverage
Trace

misconceptions.feedback: Stop is the pause at the start, when you ask what you already know. It does not take you anywhere.
Investigating the source finds out who made the page. The statistic's original is something else to look for.
Finding better coverage looks for other sources that report the same claim. Those are further accounts and not the original.

questions.prompt: A headline says a drug "halves the risk" of a rare event. The risk falls from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000. Out of 1,000 people treated, roughly how many are spared the event?
hints: Compare the two rates for the same 1,000 people.
2 per 1,000 before and 1 per 1,000 after.
questions.onCorrect: One person in a thousand is the whole benefit, which is a much smaller thing than a headline about halving suggests.

misconceptions.feedback: Halving applies to the risk, and the risk was only 2 in every 1,000 to begin with, so half of it is a very small number of people.
That would need the risk to fall by about a tenth of the group, as it would going from 20 in 100 to 10 in 100. Here it falls from 2 to 1 in every 1,000.
The two rates are enough. With 2 in 1,000 before and 1 in 1,000 after, the difference across 1,000 people can be read straight off them.

choices.label: About one person
About 500, half of the group
About 100
It cannot be estimated without the study's full data

questions.prompt: Risk falls from 8 in 1,000 to 6 in 1,000. What is the relative reduction, in percent?
hints: A relative reduction compares the fall with the old rate.
Divide the fall by the old rate.
The fall is 2, and the old rate is 8.
questions.onCorrect: The new rate is three quarters of the old one, and like any relative figure the 25% says nothing about how big the old rate was.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the absolute reduction in percentage points. The relative reduction divides the fall by the old rate.
That is the new rate as a share of the old one. The relative reduction is the fall, 2, divided by the old rate, 8.

questions.prompt: Risk falls from 40 in 100 to 20 in 100. How many people must be treated for one to benefit? (The number needed to treat.)
hints: The absolute reduction is the old rate minus the new rate, as a proportion.
40 in 100 is 0.40, and 20 in 100 is 0.20, so the reduction is 0.20.
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by that reduction.
questions.onCorrect: Five treated people give one extra benefit, so a fall of 20 percentage points is a far larger real effect than a fall of 0.1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the relative reduction as a percentage. The number needed to treat comes from the absolute reduction.
That is the group size. Use 1 divided by the absolute reduction.

questions.prompt: A survey of people's existing habits finds that coffee drinkers live longer. What kind of claim can that survey support?
hints: Did the researchers decide who drank coffee, or only record it?
What could be true of coffee drinkers other than coffee?
questions.onCorrect: An observational design can show that two things go together, but only assigning the exposure, ideally by chance, rules out the other explanations.

choices.label: That drinking coffee makes people live longer
That drinking coffee is linked to living longer
Nothing, because the researchers assigned nobody
That a randomised experiment found a benefit

acceptedIdeas: That drinking coffee is linked to living longer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That drinking coffee is linked to living longer

misconceptions.feedback: The researchers recorded who drank coffee and did not assign it, so other differences between drinkers and non-drinkers could produce the same pattern.
A survey does find real patterns, and it supports a claim of the kind its design can carry.
A randomised experiment needs people to be assigned to groups by chance, and a survey of existing habits assigns nobody.

questions.prompt: A trial reports that a treatment lowers risk from 5 in 100 to 4 in 100. What is the relative reduction, in percent?
hints: Subtract first, then divide by the old rate.
The fall is 1 in 100, and the old rate is 5 in 100.
1 divided by 5.
questions.onCorrect: The same relative figure can come from very different absolute changes, so ask for both before you decide how large the effect is.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the absolute reduction in percentage points. Divide the fall by the old rate for the relative reduction.

questions.prompt: Risk falls from 10 in 100 to 6 in 100. What is the relative reduction, in percent?
hints: Subtract, then divide by the old rate.
The fall is 4 in 100 and the old rate is 10 in 100.
4 divided by 10.
questions.onCorrect: A relative reduction of 40% compares the fall of 4 with the old rate of 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the absolute reduction in percentage points. Divide the fall by the old rate.

questions.prompt: Risk falls from 10 in 100 to 6 in 100. What is the number needed to treat?
hints: Work out the absolute reduction as a proportion.
10% minus 6% is 4%, or 0.04.
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by 0.04.
questions.onCorrect: Twenty-five people must be treated for one to benefit, since each treated person carries a 0.04 chance of being the one helped.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the relative reduction as a percentage. The number needed to treat uses the absolute reduction.
That is the absolute reduction in percentage points. Take 1 divided by it as a proportion.

questions.prompt: A study in which the researchers themselves assign people to groups, by chance, and then compare outcomes is called a what?
hints: Researchers change something and watch what follows.
The alternative is an observational study, where nothing is assigned.
questions.onCorrect: Assignment by chance spreads other differences evenly across the groups, which is why an experiment can support a causal claim where a survey cannot.

questions.prompt: Which search is best for finding research on teenagers and sleep? An asterisk matches any ending, so teen* finds teen, teens and teenagers, and adolescen* finds adolescent and adolescents.
hints: Which query names the group in more than one way and then requires sleep as well?
Synonyms of one idea go together with OR.
questions.onCorrect: Words for one idea are joined with OR to widen the net, and different ideas are joined with AND to bring the results back to your question.

choices.label: teen* AND adolescen* AND sleep
(teen* OR adolescen*) NOT sleep
teen* OR adolescen* OR sleep
(teen* OR adolescen*) AND sleep

misconceptions.feedback: Joining two words for the same group with AND asks for records that use both words, which throws away every article that uses only one of them.
NOT removes every record that mentions sleep, and sleep is the topic you want.
Joining sleep to the group with OR returns anything about sleep and anything about teenagers, a far wider set than research on the two together.

questions.prompt: Search A returns 100 results, search B returns 80, and 30 results appear in both. How many results does A OR B return?
hints: Results in both searches are in A and in B, so adding 100 and 80 counts them twice.
100 + 80 counts the 30 shared results two times.
Add the two counts, then subtract the 30 that were counted twice.
questions.onCorrect: OR returns everything in either set, and the shared results are counted once, so the total is 150 and not 180.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the 30 shared results twice. Subtract them once.
That is the number in both, which is what AND returns.

questions.prompt: Search A has 60 results, B has 45 and 15 are in both. How many results does A NOT B return?
hints: NOT removes from A everything that also appears in B.
The 15 that are in both must come out of A.
60 minus 15.
questions.onCorrect: A NOT B keeps the results in A that are not also in B, so 60 − 15 = 45.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds A and B, which counts the 15 shared results twice. NOT removes the shared results from A.
That is B NOT A. The question starts from A, and only the 15 shared results are removed from it.

questions.prompt: Searches A and B return 100 and 80 results, and 30 are in both. How many results does B NOT A return?
hints: This time you start from B and remove what is also in A.
Take the 30 shared results out of 80.
80 minus 30.
questions.onCorrect: The order matters: B NOT A keeps B's own 50, while A NOT B would keep A's 70.

misconceptions.feedback: That is A NOT B. The question starts from B.

questions.prompt: Search A returns 120 results, search B returns 90, and 40 are in both. How many does A OR B return?
hints: Add the two counts, then correct for the overlap.
120 + 90 counts the shared results twice.
Subtract the 40 once.
questions.onCorrect: OR counts each result once, so 120 + 90 − 40 = 170.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the 40 shared results twice.

questions.prompt: Search A returns 120 results, search B returns 90, and 40 are in both. How many does A NOT B return?
hints: Remove from A the results that are also in B.
The overlap is 40.
120 minus 40.
questions.onCorrect: A NOT B takes the shared 40 away from A's 120, which leaves 80.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B NOT A. The question starts from A.

questions.prompt: Which Boolean operator widens a search?
hints: Think about which joiner gives you a larger set of results than a single word does.
Two of the three joiners can only leave the set as it is, and may shrink it.
questions.onCorrect: OR joins synonyms so that a record using any of them is found, which is why it widens the search.

acceptedIdeas: OR, which returns records that contain either word
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: OR, which returns records that contain either word

choices.label: AND, which returns only records that contain both words
OR, which returns records that contain either word
NOT, which removes records that contain the excluded word

misconceptions.feedback: A record has to match both words to be returned, so each added word shrinks the set of results.
Removing every record that contains a word leaves a smaller set than the one you started with.

questions.prompt: Writing a word as its stem plus an asterisk, as in educat*, so that a search matches education, educator and educated, is called what? One word.
hints: It cuts the word short and lets the endings vary.
The word starts with "trunc".
questions.onCorrect: Truncation finds every word that starts with the same stem, so it saves you from listing each ending, though a stem too short brings in unrelated words.

questions.prompt: Following a good source's own references backward, and the later papers that cite it forward, is called citation what?
hints: The sources are linked one to the next.
A chain has links.
questions.onCorrect: Chaining uses one good source to find others, backward through its reference list and forward through the papers that cite it.

questions.prompt: The original sentence is "Seedlings grown in low light stretch toward the window faster than those grown in bright light." Which of these rewrites keeps its structure and changes only a few words?
hints: Compare the order of ideas in each version with the original.
Which one could be laid over the original, phrase by phrase?
questions.onCorrect: Changing a few words while keeping the original's order and structure leaves the sentence too close to the original to count as your own words.

choices.label: Plants kept in dim conditions reach for the glass sooner than brightly lit plants do
The passage reports that the amount of light a plant gets changes how it grows toward a window
Seedlings raised in low light grow toward the window faster than ones raised in bright light
I wonder whether older plants would lean toward the window faster in low light too

acceptedIdeas: Seedlings raised in low light grow toward the window faster than ones raised in bright light
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Seedlings raised in low light grow toward the window faster than ones raised in bright light

misconceptions.feedback: This one changes the words and the order of the idea as well, so it is a genuine restatement. Whether it counts as a paraphrase also depends on the source being named.
That is a short account of what the passage is about, and it does not rewrite the sentence at all.
That is the reader's own question and says nothing of what the source reported, so it is a comment and not a rewrite.

questions.prompt: Altering a few words of a source while keeping its structure, so that the result is not a true paraphrase, is called what? One word.
hints: It is a patch over the original, not a new text.
The word begins with "patch".
questions.onCorrect: The patched version still follows the original phrase by phrase, so it needs quotation marks or a real rewrite, and in either case it needs a citation.

questions.prompt: Exact words copied from a source must be put inside what marks?
hints: They show a reader, and your later self, that the words are not yours.
Two small marks enclose the copied words.
questions.onCorrect: Quotation marks are the signal that the words are the source's, and without them a note can later pass for your own wording.

questions.prompt: The second note reads "Plants kept in dim conditions reach for the glass sooner than brightly lit plants do", with Lee 2019, p. 14 as its source. What kind of note is it?
hints: It keeps the idea and changes the wording and the structure.
Ask whether it covers one passage or the whole source.
questions.onCorrect: A paraphrase keeps the idea and changes the words and the structure, and it still needs the source, since the idea is not yours.

choices.label: Quotation
Summary
Paraphrase
Comment

misconceptions.feedback: A quotation copies the source's exact words inside quotation marks. These words are new.
A summary shortens a whole source or section to its main points. This note restates the idea of one sentence.
A comment is your own reaction to the passage, kept apart from what the source says. This note reports what the source says.

questions.prompt: A note for a quotation gives the author and the year in its source line. What other detail lets a reader find the passage again?
hints: Where in the source does the passage sit?
A quotation especially needs this.
questions.onCorrect: The page lets you, or a reader, go straight back to the passage to check it, which is what a citation is for.

questions.prompt: Next to a passage you write in your notes: "This ignores older plants." Which type of note is it?
hints: Does it say what the source reported, or what you think of it?
questions.onCorrect: A comment is your own reaction, and labelling it as one keeps your view from being taken later for the source's claim.

choices.label: Paraphrase
Comment
Summary
Quotation

misconceptions.feedback: A paraphrase restates the source's idea in your own words. This note does not say what the source reported, because it reacts to it.
A summary shortens what the source says. This note adds a view of your own.
A quotation gives the source's exact words inside quotation marks. This note is not the source's wording.

questions.prompt: Which of these is patchwriting of "Seedlings grown in low light stretch toward the window faster than those grown in bright light"?
hints: Which version follows the original phrase by phrase?
Look for a version that swaps a word and keeps the order.
questions.onCorrect: The patched version swaps "grown" for "raised" and "stretch" for "grow" and otherwise follows the original, so it is too close to count as a paraphrase.

choices.label: Plants kept in dim conditions reach for the glass sooner than brightly lit plants do
I think light matters
The article is about plants
Seedlings raised in low light grow toward the window faster than ones raised in bright light

acceptedIdeas: Seedlings raised in low light grow toward the window faster than ones raised in bright light
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Seedlings raised in low light grow toward the window faster than ones raised in bright light

misconceptions.feedback: This one restates the idea in a new wording and a new structure, so it is a paraphrase, provided the source is credited.
That is the reader's own opinion, which is a comment.
That is a very short summary of the topic, not a copy of the sentence.

questions.prompt: Exact words copied from a source must be put in what marks? Two words.
hints: The marks tell a reader the words belong to someone else.
Two small marks enclose the copied words.
questions.onCorrect: Unmarked copying cannot be told apart from your own writing once the note is a month old, which is how plagiarism happens by accident.

questions.prompt: A short account of the main points of a whole source, in your own words, is a what?
hints: It condenses a long text to its main points.
A paraphrase restates one passage, whereas this condenses the whole.
questions.onCorrect: A summary shortens a source to its main points, so it is far shorter than the original and still needs the source named.

questions.prompt: A synthesis says what several sources show together. A paragraph describes Source A, then Source B, then Source C, one after another. What is it?
hints: What organises the paragraph: the ideas, or the sources?
Does anything in it say how A, B and C relate?
questions.onCorrect: Moving from source to source without comparing them leaves the sources side by side, which is a summary. The comparing is the synthesis.

choices.label: A synthesis, since it brings in every source that was read
A summary of each source, with the comparing left undone
A comparison, since the sources sit side by side

acceptedIdeas: A summary of each source, with the comparing left undone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A summary of each source, with the comparing left undone

misconceptions.feedback: A synthesis is organised by ideas and says what the sources show together. Describing them one at a time leaves that work for the reader.
Putting sources one after another is not comparing them. Nothing in the paragraph says how A, B and C relate.

questions.prompt: Five more invented studies had 300, 150, 80, 1,200 and 70 participants. How many participants were there in total?
hints: Add the five sample sizes.
300 + 150 + 80 = 530, then add the other two.
questions.onCorrect: The total is the base for judging how much of the evidence each group of studies carries, which is the next step.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the three benefit studies only. Add the other two.
That leaves out the three benefit studies. Add all five.

questions.prompt: Another five invented studies had 350, 200, 160, 1,500 and 60 participants, and the three that found a benefit had 350, 200 and 160. How many participants were in studies that found a benefit?
hints: Add the sample sizes of the three studies that found a benefit.
The third study adds 160 more.
questions.onCorrect: The three benefit studies hold only 710 of the 2,270 participants, about 31%, though they are three of the five studies.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total across all five studies. Count only the three that found a benefit.

questions.prompt: Judging a question by how many sources agree, and ignoring the size and quality of each, is called what? Two words.
hints: Each source gets one vote, however large or small it is.
It is how an election counts, but evidence is not an election.
questions.onCorrect: Three of five studies favour a benefit, yet they hold about 27% of the participants, so counting each study as one vote overstates the support.

questions.prompt: The three benefit studies hold 770 of the 2,860 participants. How many participants were in the studies that found no benefit or found harm?
hints: The rest of the participants are in the other two studies.
Subtract 770 from 2,860.
Or add the other two samples, 2,000 and 90.
questions.onCorrect: Most of the participants, 2,090 of them, were in studies that did not find a benefit, which changes how much the three positive studies can carry.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the benefit studies. The question asks about the other two.

questions.prompt: Another set of five invented studies had 500, 300, 100, 1,600 and 200 participants. How many participants were there in total?
hints: Add the five sample sizes.
questions.onCorrect: A total across studies is the starting point for asking how much of the evidence each group of studies holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first three only. Add all five.

questions.prompt: In that second set the three studies with 500, 300 and 100 participants found a benefit, and the 1,600 and 200 found none. How many participants were in studies that found a benefit?
hints: Count only the three that found a benefit.
Add 100.
questions.onCorrect: The benefit studies hold 900 of 2,700 participants, a third, though they are three of the five studies.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every participant. Count only the three that found a benefit.

questions.prompt: Treating a question as settled because most of the studies agree, whatever their size, is called what? Two words.
hints: Each study is counted once, large or small.
It is an election, where every vote weighs the same.
questions.onCorrect: Counting studies gives a small trial the same say as a large one, and weighing them corrects that.

questions.prompt: Which of these needs a citation in a piece of writing?
hints: Which one could a reader reasonably ask you to back up?
A figure from one particular survey comes from that survey and no other.
questions.onCorrect: A number from one survey came from that survey, so the reader needs to be told which one, whereas facts known everywhere need no source.

choices.label: Two plus two is four
A statistic from a survey
Paris is in France
Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level

misconceptions.feedback: That is common knowledge: it is widely known and easy to find in many sources, so it needs no citation.
That is common knowledge and is found in countless sources, so a reader would not ask where you got it.
That is a fact so familiar that no source is needed, and no reader would ask where you got it.

questions.prompt: A persistent identifier that resolves to a published work, so that a reader can find it, is abbreviated to three letters. What are they?
hints: The first word of its full name is digital.
A reference often ends with a code beginning with the number 10.
questions.onCorrect: A DOI stays the same when a publisher redesigns its website, which is why a link built on it keeps working where an ordinary web address may not.

questions.prompt: In the reference "Lee, J. (2019). Light and seedling growth. Journal of Plant Studies, 12(3), 14-29.", which part is "Journal of Plant Studies"?
hints: The article sits inside it, along with others.
The part's name covers a journal, a book or a website alike.
questions.onCorrect: The container is the larger work an article sits in, and many styles name it as a part of the reference since it is where a reader looks for the article.

choices.label: The title
The publisher
The container
The volume

misconceptions.feedback: The title is the name of the article itself, Light and seedling growth. The journal is the larger work that holds it.
A publisher is the company that issues a journal, and this reference does not name one. Journal of Plant Studies is the journal itself.
The volume is the number that follows the journal's name, 12. The name itself plays another part.

questions.prompt: The reference ends "Journal of Plant Studies, 12(3)." Which part is missing, so that a reader cannot find the article within the issue?
hints: Volume and issue say which book of the journal. What says where in it?
It is a range such as 14 to 29.
questions.onCorrect: The pages let a reader turn straight to the article in the volume, which is the point of listing a volume at all.

questions.prompt: An AI tool gives you a reference with an author, a title and a journal, but you cannot find the paper in any database or on the journal's site. What should you do with it?
hints: Tools can produce references that look right and name papers that do not exist.
What have you not been able to do?
questions.onCorrect: A reference that cannot be found has not been shown to exist, so it stays out of your list until you have located the paper itself.

acceptedIdeas: Treat it as unverified and leave it out until you have found the paper
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Treat it as unverified and leave it out until you have found the paper

choices.label: Cite it with a note saying you could not find the paper
Keep the author and journal and replace the title with one you can find
Treat it as unverified and leave it out until you have found the paper
Use it, since a reference with all its parts in place is very likely real

misconceptions.feedback: A well-formed reference shows only that the tool can produce the format. Tools can produce plausible references to papers that do not exist.
A reader would then be sent to look for a paper that may not exist. A reference is there so the reader can find the work, which this one cannot yet do.
That would cite a different work under the first one's details. Either the paper you meant is found, or the reference goes.

questions.prompt: A reference ends in a code that begins with 10. and takes a reader to the published work, even after the publisher redesigns its website. What is the code called? Use the three-letter abbreviation.
hints: It is a persistent identifier for the work, so it can be found again.
The first word of its full name is digital.
questions.onCorrect: A DOI identifies a published work in a way that outlasts changes to where it is hosted.

questions.prompt: A writer uses a statistic from a particular survey. Does it need a citation?
hints: Could a reader find the figure in many sources, or in one?
A number from one survey came from that survey.
questions.onCorrect: Data comes from a particular source, and the citation tells the reader which one so they can check it.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because the figure belongs to that survey and a reader can only check it there
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because the figure belongs to that survey and a reader can only check it there

choices.label: Only if it is quoted word for word from the survey's report
Yes, because the figure belongs to that survey and a reader can only check it there
No, because numbers are facts and facts need no citation

misconceptions.feedback: Common knowledge is a fact found in many places. A figure from one survey is found in one place, so the reader needs to be told which.
Quotation is only one of the things that need a source. Data needs one too, however you word the sentence around it.

questions.prompt: You are writing one essay and citing twelve sources. What should you do about citation style?
hints: Is a style a matter of taste within one piece, or a system that works only if it is used consistently?
Consider what the reader has to do to follow the references.
questions.onCorrect: A style is a system for ordering the same parts, and using it consistently lets a reader learn the pattern once.

choices.label: Use one style consistently throughout the piece
Use footnotes for some and brackets for others
Choose whichever format you like for each source
Leave out the year when it is awkward

acceptedIdeas: Use one style consistently throughout the piece
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use one style consistently throughout the piece

misconceptions.feedback: A reader who meets a different format at each source has to work out each one, and a mixed list looks as if nobody checked it.
Every style needs the year, because it tells the reader which edition or version of a work you are using.
Styles are systems, and mixing parts of two of them leaves a reader unsure how to read any of them.

questions.prompt: Four invented studies tested a reading programme. One, with 1,500 pupils, found a benefit, and three, with 60, 80 and 100 pupils, found none. A summary says that most studies find the programme does not work. What is wrong with that summary?
hints: Add up how many pupils were in the three studies that found nothing.
Compare that with the 1,500 in the one study that found a benefit.
questions.onCorrect: Weighing by size reverses the count here, and a synthesis would still ask how each study was designed before resting much on the large one.

choices.label: Nothing is wrong: three of the four studies found no benefit, a clear majority
It should have averaged the four results, so that each study counts equally
It should have dropped the three small studies, since small studies prove nothing
It counts studies and ignores that one study holds most of the pupils

acceptedIdeas: It counts studies and ignores that one study holds most of the pupils
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It counts studies and ignores that one study holds most of the pupils

misconceptions.feedback: That is vote counting. Three studies agree, but between them they hold 240 of the 1,740 pupils, so treating them as three votes against one overstates their weight.
Counting each study equally is the summary's own mistake, only expressed as an average. Size and design are what should set each study's weight.
Small studies are weaker guides, but they are still evidence, and a synthesis says what it did with them instead of dropping them without a word.

questions.prompt: Claim: libraries should open on Sundays. Grounds: most people work on weekdays. Which of these, added to the claim, is a qualifier?
hints: A qualifier limits how far the claim reaches.
Ask which phrase narrows the claim, and which phrases do some other job.

acceptedIdeas: in towns with more than 20,000 people
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: in towns with more than 20,000 people

questions.onCorrect: A qualifier marks how far the claim is meant to reach, and a claim that states its limits is easier to defend.

choices.label: unless the council cannot pay for the extra staff
in towns with more than 20,000 people
because most people work on weekdays
assuming that people who work on weekdays would visit on Sundays

misconceptions.feedback: That names a condition under which the claim would fail, which makes it a rebuttal. A qualifier narrows how far the claim reaches without saying when it fails.
That is the evidence offered for the claim, which makes it the grounds. A qualifier changes the claim itself.
That is the assumption linking the grounds to the claim, which makes it the warrant. A qualifier limits how far the claim reaches.

questions.prompt: In the argument that the town should run a bus to the hospital, because many patients miss appointments for lack of a car, which of these is the rebuttal?
hints: A rebuttal names a case in which the claim would not hold.
Ask which statement a critic of the argument would offer.

acceptedIdeas: Unless most of those patients live too far from a bus route
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Unless most of those patients live too far from a bus route

questions.onCorrect: A rebuttal names a case in which the claim would not hold, and saying it yourself shows you have tested the argument.

choices.label: Many patients miss appointments because they have no car
A bus would get patients without a car to their appointments
Unless most of those patients live too far from a bus route
Towns that added hospital buses saw fewer missed appointments

misconceptions.feedback: That is the evidence offered for the claim, which makes it the grounds. A rebuttal names a condition under which the claim would fail.
That is the assumption linking the grounds to the claim, which makes it the warrant. A rebuttal says when that link would break.
That is evidence supporting the warrant, which makes it the backing. A rebuttal works against the claim and not for it.

questions.prompt: In "Shaded streets stay cooler, so trees reduce illness", the word "so" is an indicator word. What does it tell you?
hints: Ask which of the two statements is meant to support the other.

acceptedIdeas: The statement after it follows from the one before it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The statement after it follows from the one before it

questions.onCorrect: Because, since and for introduce reasons, and so, therefore and thus introduce what follows from them.

choices.label: The statement after it follows from the one before it
The statement after it is a reason for the one before it
The statement before it is the author's main claim
The two statements say the same thing in other words

misconceptions.feedback: That is the direction of *because* and *since*, which point back to a reason. The word *so* points forward to what follows.
A claim is what the other statements work to support. The statement before *so* is doing that supporting, which makes it a reason and not the conclusion.
If the two said the same thing, *so* would have nothing to join. It links a reason to something that follows from it.

questions.prompt: Claim: the museum should open late on Fridays. Grounds: most visitors say they work until five. Which unstated assumption links the two?
hints: Ask what has to be true for the visitors' working hours to count as a reason for opening later.
Which answer joins the grounds to the claim?

acceptedIdeas: Visitors who work until five would come if it opened later
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Visitors who work until five would come if it opened later

questions.onCorrect: The argument needs working visitors to come if the opening hours change, and nothing in the passage says so, which is why it counts as an assumption.

choices.label: The museum could afford the extra staff for the later hours
Most other museums in the region already stay open late
People who work all day enjoy visiting museums in the evening
Visitors who work until five would come if it opened later

misconceptions.feedback: Cost is a practical matter. It does not connect working visitors to a later closing time.
What other museums do is a different kind of support. It does not connect the visitors' working hours to this museum's opening.
Enjoying evening visits is not what the grounds are about. The gap lies between working until five and being able to come.

questions.prompt: You need this year's published unemployment figures. Which of these is the best place to get them?
hints: Which of these is closest to the data itself?
A summary written earlier cannot contain this year's figures.

acceptedIdeas: The statistics office's own published table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The statistics office's own published table

questions.onCorrect: A government data table is the primary evidence for a figure, and any summary of it is a step further away.

choices.label: A textbook chapter on the labour market
A news feature on what the jobs figures mean
A review article on unemployment research
The statistics office's own published table

misconceptions.feedback: A textbook sums up what a field has settled on, so it lags behind this year's figures and sits two steps from the data.
A feature reports and interprets the figures, so you get someone else's choice of numbers and not the table itself.
A review article analyses studies that are already published, so it cannot hold this year's figures, and it sits a step away from the data.

questions.prompt: A page says "studies show that supplement X improves memory", and it links to one study. Having checked who made the page and looked for independent reports, what is the next move?
hints: Which move goes back to the original of a claim?
The page gives a link, so ask what is at the other end of it.

acceptedIdeas: Open the study and compare what it found with what the page says
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Open the study and compare what it found with what the page says

questions.onCorrect: Tracing takes you from the report of a claim to its origin, where you can see what was originally said and in what context.

choices.label: Open the study and compare what it found with what the page says
Accept the claim, since the page cites a study
Search for other pages that repeat the same claim
Read the Institute's About page to see how it describes the study

misconceptions.feedback: A citation shows only that the page names a study. The page may have chosen it, quoted it selectively or misread it.
Other pages repeating a claim show how widely it is told, but they do not show what the study found.
The About page is the site's own account of itself, and it cannot show what the study found.

questions.prompt: Search A has 70 results, B has 45 and 15 are in both. How many results does A NOT B return?
hints: NOT removes from A everything that also appears in B.
The 15 that are in both must come out of A.
70 minus 15.
questions.onCorrect: A NOT B keeps the results in A that are not also in B, so 70 − 15 = 55.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds A and B, which counts the 15 shared results twice. NOT removes the shared results from A.
That is B NOT A. The question starts from A, and only the 15 shared results are removed from it.
That is the size of B. A NOT B starts from A and takes the shared results out of it.

questions.prompt: You copy one sentence from an article into your notes, word for word. What must the note show?
hints: Ask what you, a month from now, could tell from the note about whose words they are.

acceptedIdeas: Quotation marks around the words, with the source and page
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Quotation marks around the words, with the source and page

questions.onCorrect: Quotation marks signal that the words are the source's, and without them a note can later pass for your own wording.

choices.label: Quotation marks around the words, with the source and page
The source and page alone, since that shows whose idea it is
A few changed words, so that the note is in your own words

misconceptions.feedback: A source and page say where the idea came from, but without quotation marks the words themselves will later look like yours.
Changing a few words is patchwriting, which is neither a quotation nor a paraphrase, and the note still needs its source.

questions.prompt: Which of these is patchwriting of "Bees visit flowers close to the hive more often than flowers that are far from it"?
hints: Which version follows the original phrase by phrase?
Look for a version that swaps a word and keeps the order.

acceptedIdeas: Bees visit flowers near the hive more often than flowers that lie far from it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bees visit flowers near the hive more often than flowers that lie far from it

questions.onCorrect: The patched version swaps "close to" for "near" and otherwise follows the original, so it is too close to count as a paraphrase.

choices.label: Bees visit flowers near the hive more often than flowers that lie far from it
The nearer a flower grows to the hive, the more often bees visit it
The passage reports that the distance between hive and flower affects how often bees visit
I wonder whether wasps also visit nearby flowers more often than distant ones

misconceptions.feedback: This one restates the idea in a new wording and a new structure, so it is a paraphrase, provided the source is credited.
That is a short account of what the passage is about, and it does not copy the sentence.
That is the reader's own question, which is a comment.

questions.prompt: An AI tool gives you five references. You search a database and find papers matching the first, third and fourth, but nothing at all for the second and fifth. What should your reference list contain?
hints: Tools can produce references that look right and name papers that do not exist.
Which of the five have you actually seen?

acceptedIdeas: Only the three you found, until you locate the other two
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the three you found, until you locate the other two

questions.onCorrect: A reference that cannot be found has not been shown to exist, so it stays out of your list until you have located the paper itself.

choices.label: All five, since the tool wrote each one in the correct form
All five, with a note beside the two that you could not find
Only the three you found, until you locate the other two

misconceptions.feedback: A well-formed reference shows only that the tool can produce the format. Tools can produce plausible references to papers that do not exist.
A reader would then be sent to look for papers that may not exist. A reference is there so the reader can find the work, which these two cannot yet do.

questions.prompt: A writer explains, in their own words and their own structure, an argument that they read in a book. Does the explanation need a citation?
hints: A citation lets a reader check the work and gives credit to the person who did it.
Ask who had the idea first.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because the idea came from the book, whoever words it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because the idea came from the book, whoever words it

questions.onCorrect: A paraphrase restates someone else's idea, so the citation credits the idea and lets a reader go back to check it.

choices.label: Yes, because the idea came from the book, whoever words it
No, because the writer has put the idea in their own words
Only if it repeats the book's exact words, as only copying needs one

misconceptions.feedback: A paraphrase changes the words and keeps the idea, and the idea is the book's. A reader still needs to be able to check it, and the author still deserves the credit.
Quotation is only one of the things that need a source. A paraphrase and a distinctive idea need one too, however the sentence is worded.

questions.prompt: An essay cites twelve sources. Some of the references were copied from publishers' websites, each in the style that site uses, and the rest were typed by hand. What should the finished list look like?
hints: Think about the person who has to read the whole list.

acceptedIdeas: All twelve in one style, reformatting those that differ
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All twelve in one style, reformatting those that differ

questions.onCorrect: A style is a system for ordering the same parts, and using one consistently lets a reader learn the pattern once.

choices.label: Each reference in the style it arrived in, since every part is present
All twelve in one style, reformatting those that differ
Each reference in its publisher's style, so that it matches the journal

misconceptions.feedback: Having every part is not enough. A list in mixed styles makes the reader work out the pattern again at each entry.
The publisher's style belongs to the publisher's own pages. Your list is one document, and its reader needs one pattern.

flashcards.front: In SQ3R, which step comes between Survey and Read?
flashcards.back: Question: turning headings into questions gives the reading a job to do.

flashcards.front: A 300-page book, 25 pages a day: how many days?
flashcards.back: Pages divided by pages per day gives 12 days.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Pages divided by pages per day gives 12 days.

flashcards.front: Before you start a text, what question decides how you read it?
flashcards.back: Why am I reading this: your purpose decides how deeply and in what order you read.

flashcards.front: What do you call the assumption linking grounds to claim?
flashcards.back: The warrant: it is usually unstated, and finding it shows where an argument could fail.

flashcards.front: Name the claim, grounds and warrant of the last op-ed you read.
flashcards.back: Saying all three from memory shows you can separate what the author wants from what supports it.

flashcards.front: Which indicator word introduces a reason: "because" or "therefore"?
flashcards.back: Because introduces a reason, while therefore introduces the conclusion that follows from it.

flashcards.front: What do you call the feeling of knowing that a familiar page gives you?
flashcards.back: The fluency illusion: a page you recognise reads smoothly, which does not show you can recall it.

flashcards.front: Read on 3 November: which November date is the 14-day review?
flashcards.back: 3 + 14 = 17, so the review falls on 17 November.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 + 14 = 17, so the review falls on 17 November.

flashcards.front: Close the book now and write three sentences about what you last read. How well could you do it?
flashcards.back: Writing from memory is retrieval practice, and what you could not say shows what to study again.

flashcards.front: Primary, secondary or tertiary: a review article analysing many studies?
flashcards.back: Secondary: it analyses primary sources, and a tertiary source would only summarise such analyses.

flashcards.front: What does peer review guarantee about a paper?
flashcards.back: Only that other experts judged it fit to publish, and not that it is correct, since reviewers seldom repeat the work.

flashcards.front: Which kind of source is a good first stop for an overview of a field you do not know?
flashcards.back: A tertiary source such as a textbook or encyclopaedia, which summarises the field and points to its sources.

flashcards.front: Which SIFT move comes first?
flashcards.back: Stop: ask what you know about the source before you read on.

flashcards.front: Why is a site's own About page weak evidence about the site?
flashcards.back: Because the site wrote it, so it is the site speaking about itself, and independent evidence has to come from elsewhere.

flashcards.front: Name the habit of leaving a page to see what others say about its source.
flashcards.back: Lateral reading: you open new tabs to check the source before you read the page closely.

flashcards.front: A risk falls from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000. What is the relative reduction, in percent?
flashcards.back: The fall of 1 is half of the old rate of 2, so the relative reduction is 50%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fall of 1 is half of the old rate of 2, so the relative reduction is 50%.

flashcards.front: Risk falls from 20 in 100 to 10 in 100. What is the number needed to treat?
flashcards.back: The absolute reduction is 0.10, and 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10 people.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The absolute reduction is 0.10, and 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10 people.

flashcards.front: Why is "halves the risk" not enough to say a treatment matters?
flashcards.back: Because a halving of a tiny risk can be a tiny absolute change, so you need the absolute change and the number needed to treat as well.

flashcards.front: Which Boolean operator joins synonyms to widen a search?
flashcards.back: OR: a record using any of the words is returned, so it widens the search.

flashcards.front: A: 100 results, B: 80, both: 30. How many does A AND B return?
flashcards.back: AND returns only the results in both, which is 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AND returns only the results in both, which is 30.

flashcards.front: Why do you not join two synonyms with AND?
flashcards.back: Because AND requires both words to appear, so you lose every record that uses only one of them.

flashcards.front: What is patchwriting?
flashcards.back: Altering a few words of a source while keeping its structure, which is not a paraphrase and still needs quotation marks or a rewrite.

flashcards.front: What marks must exact copied words carry in your notes?
flashcards.back: Quotation marks, because they tell your later self that the words are not yours.

flashcards.front: Take a note on the last thing you read: type, text, source with page and your own comment. Does each part of the card have its own place?
flashcards.back: Keeping the source's words, your rewording and your own view apart is what lets you reuse the note without mistaking whose it is.

flashcards.front: What is vote counting?
flashcards.back: Judging a question by how many sources agree, ignoring the size and quality of each study.

flashcards.front: Five studies: 400, 250 and 120 found a benefit; 2,000 found none; 90 found harm. How many participants in all?
flashcards.back: The five sample sizes add to 2,860.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The five sample sizes add to 2,860.

flashcards.front: How is a synthesis different from a summary of each source in turn?
flashcards.back: A synthesis is organised by ideas and says what the sources show together, including where they disagree, whereas a summary takes the sources one by one.

flashcards.front: What is a DOI?
flashcards.back: A persistent identifier that resolves to a published work, so a reader can find it even if the web address changes.

flashcards.front: A reference lists author, year, title, journal, volume and pages. What does a DOI add?
flashcards.back: A link to the work that does not break when a website moves, so a reader can find the exact paper.

flashcards.front: A tool gave you a reference you cannot find in any database. Why must you leave it out until you verify it?
flashcards.back: Tools can produce references that look correct and name papers that do not exist, so a reference only counts once you have found the work itself.
